It pulls in product usage data, support tickets, and CRM information to give each account a health score, so a team can see which customers are thriving and which are at risk of leaving before a renewal conversation turns bad.

Automation handles routine outreach. Playbooks trigger tasks and emails when a customer hits a milestone or goes quiet, in-app messages guide users inside the product, and dashboards track renewals, adoption, and revenue. AI features summarize accounts, draft messages, and suggest next actions, and a customer-facing portal can share progress with clients.

item.title: Cognism
item.description:
Cognism helps salespeople reach the right people. Its database covers companies and contacts across regions, with a reputation for strong coverage in Europe and for verified mobile numbers, which are valuable for cold calling. Users filter by role, industry, size, and technology, then export or sync contacts to their CRM.

Intent data adds timing. Signals show which accounts are researching topics related to a product, so teams can prioritize outreach. Compliance is a selling point: the company screens contacts against do-not-call lists and says it follows privacy rules like GDPR, which matters for outreach in Europe.

item.title: Databricks
item.description:
Databricks started with Apache Spark and grew into a unified platform for data work. Companies store data in open formats in their cloud, then use Databricks for pipelines, SQL analytics, notebooks, and machine learning, with a governance layer called Unity Catalog that controls access and tracks lineage across it all.

AI has become central to the pitch. The platform supports training and fine-tuning models, serving them through endpoints, vector search for retrieval, and a framework for building agents grounded in enterprise data. The company acquired MosaicML to strengthen model training, and offers tools to monitor and evaluate AI systems. An assistant helps write code and queries.

item.title: Gainsight
item.description:
Gainsight was one of the first platforms for the customer success discipline. It pulls usage, support, survey, and billing data to produce a health score for every customer, so teams can see who needs attention before a renewal is at risk. Playbooks guide the steps a manager should take for each situation.

AI features predict churn, suggest next actions, summarize account history, and draft communications. Surveys, in-app engagement, and a community product complete the suite, and the company has expanded into customer education. Reports help leaders show the effect of customer success on retention.

item.title: Glassbox
item.description:
Glassbox captures user sessions on digital properties. Teams can replay a visit to see what a customer clicked, where they hesitated, and what errors they hit. Heatmaps summarize click and scroll behavior across many sessions, pointing to confusing pages or broken flows.

The platform adds analytics and detection. Journey analysis shows where users leave a funnel, and automatic detection flags frustration signals such as repeated clicks. It has features for regulated industries like banking, including data masking so that sensitive information is not stored. The company has expanded through acquisitions into areas like anomaly detection.

item.title: Hex
item.description:
Hex combines notebooks with business intelligence. Teams connect their data warehouse, write SQL and Python in a notebook, and turn the results into interactive apps that non-technical colleagues can use without code. Everything lives in one place with version history and comments.

AI is built into the workflow. Magic helps write and fix queries and code, and agents let business users ask questions of governed data in plain language. A semantic layer keeps definitions of metrics consistent, so answers match across reports. Scheduled runs keep outputs fresh.

item.title: Highspot
item.description:
Highspot helps sales organizations make sure reps find and use the right material. Marketing publishes decks, case studies, and playbooks in one library, reps search or get recommendations based on the deal stage and customer, and managers see which assets are used and which correlate with wins.

Training and coaching tools are part of the platform, including practice exercises, call reviews, and guided selling plays. AI features recommend content, summarize accounts, and generate tailored messages and presentations. Integrations with CRMs and communication tools bring this into reps’ daily workflow.

item.title: Instapage
item.description:
Instapage focuses on the page that visitors reach after clicking an ad. Marketers build pages in a drag-and-drop editor with templates, connect them to ad campaigns, and track conversion rates. Collaboration features let teams and clients comment directly on designs.

Optimization tools set it apart. A/B testing compares versions, heatmaps show where visitors engage, and personalization changes page content depending on the ad or audience that sent the visitor. AI helps write copy and suggests improvements.

item.title: Kaspr
item.description:
Kaspr is a contact data tool for outbound sales. While browsing a LinkedIn profile, a user clicks the Kaspr extension to reveal a professional email address and phone number, then saves the contact to a CRM or a list. It also supports bulk searches and enrichment of existing records.

The company emphasizes European data and compliance with privacy rules like GDPR, and offers ways for individuals to opt out of the database. Credits limit how many contact details a user can reveal each month, and integrations connect with CRMs and sales engagement tools.

item.title: Kommunicate
item.description:
Kommunicate combines a chatbot builder with a shared inbox for agents. Businesses add a chat widget to their site or app, train a bot on help articles and FAQs, and let it answer routine questions, handing the conversation to a person when the bot cannot help or the customer asks.

The platform supports generative AI models and connects to knowledge bases, so answers draw on company content. Multi-channel support extends to messaging apps, and analytics show deflection rates and satisfaction. Integrations with CRMs and helpdesks keep data in sync.

item.title: Lusha
item.description:
Lusha helps sales and recruiting teams get in touch with prospects. While viewing a profile on LinkedIn or a company website, a user clicks the Lusha extension to reveal contact information, then saves it to a CRM. A database search finds contacts by role, company size, and industry.

Additional features include intent signals, technology data, and enrichment of existing lists, as well as integrations with Salesforce, HubSpot, and sales engagement tools. The company emphasizes compliance with privacy laws and offers ways for people to opt out.

item.title: MotherDuck
item.description:
MotherDuck takes the DuckDB analytical database, which runs on a laptop, and adds a cloud service. A user connects from their local DuckDB, queries data in the cloud, and combines it with local files, in what the company calls hybrid execution, using each machine for what it does best.

It targets teams that do not need a large data warehouse. Features include shared databases, collaboration, integrations with common data tools, and an AI assistant that helps write SQL. The pitch is simple, fast analytics at lower cost for data in the gigabytes to terabytes range.

item.title: Navattic
item.description:
Navattic helps companies show software without a live demo. A marketer captures a product’s screens or pages, adds callouts and steps, and publishes a tour that visitors can click through. Gated or ungated, these demos let prospects see the product before talking to sales.

Analytics show who viewed a demo and how far they went, giving sales a signal about interest. Personalization lets teams tailor tours by account, and integrations send engagement data to CRMs and marketing tools. AI helps create and edit demos and write copy.

item.title: Phrasee
item.description:
Phrasee focuses on the words in marketing messages. A team sets up a brand voice, and the platform generates many variations of subject lines, push text, or ads, predicts which will perform best, and tests them against audiences. Results feed back to improve future suggestions.

The company has become part of Jacquard Group, which combines it with other brand messaging tools. Large retailers, financial institutions, and travel brands used it to squeeze more from large campaigns, where small improvements in open rate add up.

item.title: Seamless AI
item.description:
Seamless.AI helps salespeople find who to contact. Users search by title, industry, and location, or use a browser extension to look up contacts on websites, and the platform returns emails and phone numbers pulled from public sources and its database. Lists export to CRMs and engagement tools.

Real-time search and enrichment aim to keep data fresh, and intent signals show which accounts may be in a buying cycle. AI features help write outreach and prioritize accounts.

item.title: Seismic
item.description:
Seismic organizes marketing and sales content so reps can find and use it. Instead of searching shared drives, a seller gets recommended decks, case studies, and playbooks based on the deal stage and customer, and can assemble personalized presentations quickly.

Analytics show which content gets used and which correlates with wins, and engagement data tells sellers how buyers interact with shared materials. Coaching and training modules, and AI that writes tailored messages and summaries, add to the suite.

item.title: Showpad
item.description:
Showpad helps sellers find and use approved content. Marketing publishes decks, videos, and guides, and reps get recommendations based on the customer and deal stage. Buyers receive shared links that track engagement, which tells sellers what resonated.

Coaching and training are the other half. Reps practice pitches and receive AI feedback, learning paths build skills, and managers see progress. The platform integrates with CRMs and works well in industries such as manufacturing, healthcare, and technology.

item.title: Snowflake
item.description:
Snowflake pioneered the cloud data warehouse built on this separation. Companies load data, run SQL queries with elastic compute, and share datasets securely with partners. It runs on the major clouds, and teams of analysts and engineers use it as a central data foundation.

The platform has grown into an AI data cloud. Cortex provides language model functions, search over documents, and agents that run inside the platform, close to the data, with governance. It also supports machine learning, Python workloads, and apps built on Snowflake data.

item.title: Supademo
item.description:
Supademo makes product demos quickly. A user records clicks through an app with a browser extension, and Supademo converts them into a step-by-step interactive demo with callouts, which can be edited, branded, and embedded on a site or emailed.

AI adds voiceover narration and translations, and helps write step text. Analytics show who viewed a demo and where they stopped. The tool is also used for onboarding guides and help documentation.

item.title: Talkwalker
item.description:
Talkwalker monitors the public conversation about brands and topics. Users set up searches, and the platform collects posts, articles, forums, and broadcast mentions from around the world, then analyzes volume, sentiment, and who is talking. Alerts flag spikes that may signal a crisis or opportunity.

Image and video recognition detect logos in pictures even when the brand name is not written, and AI summarizes themes and trends. Marketing and communications teams use the findings to measure campaigns, track competitors, and shape messaging, and a generative assistant helps analysts query the data.

item.title: Totango
item.description:
Totango helps subscription companies keep customers. It gathers usage and account data, scores health, and triggers playbooks when customers need attention. Modules called SuccessBLOCs package best-practice workflows that teams can adopt and adjust.

The company merged with Catalyst, another customer success platform, and the combined product serves teams from startups to enterprises. AI features summarize accounts and draft communications, and analytics show retention and expansion.

Totango has had a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Gainsight, ChurnZero, Planhat, Vitally, and HubSpot. Totango suits customer success teams at software companies.

item.title: Typeform
item.description:
Typeform changed the feel of online forms. Instead of showing a long page of fields, it presents one question at a time with large type and smooth transitions, which tends to make forms feel friendlier and often improves completion rates. People use it for surveys, quizzes, lead capture, registrations, feedback, and onboarding. Design options and templates make it easy to match a brand.

Behind the interface are capable features. Logic jumps change the next question based on earlier answers, calculators and scoring support quizzes, payments can be collected, and files can be uploaded. Integrations send responses to tools like Google Sheets, HubSpot, Slack, and Zapier. AI features help generate a form from a short prompt, suggest questions, and summarize responses so teams can understand results faster.

item.title: Yellow.ai
item.description:
Yellow.ai builds AI agents for customer and employee service. A company connects it to systems such as CRMs and ticketing, trains it on content, and deploys across websites, messaging apps, and phone lines. The agents answer questions and complete tasks in many languages.

The platform emphasizes multilingual support, strong in markets such as India, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Tools for building, testing, and monitoring agents, along with analytics, support operations teams. Handoff to human agents is built in.

item.title: Zumper
item.description:
Zumper lists rentals with photos, prices, and neighborhood details. Renters filter by price, bedrooms, pets, and commute, save searches, and message landlords. A universal application and tools for screening speed up the process.

Recommendations use preferences and behavior, and data on rents helps renters understand local prices. Landlords and property managers pay to list and get leads.

Zumper is free for renters. Listings can be outdated, and renters should watch for scams. Alternatives include Zillow Rentals, Apartments.com, Rent.com, Trulia, and Craigslist. Zumper suits renters in major US cities.

item.title: Looker
item.description:
Looker takes a modeling-first approach. Data teams define dimensions and measures in LookML, a code-based language, and users explore data and build dashboards on top of those shared definitions. This keeps numbers consistent and cuts arguments over whose revenue figure is right.

The platform queries data warehouses directly, so it works with the company’s data without extracting it. It supports embedded analytics, letting companies put dashboards in their own products. Gemini in Looker adds conversational analytics and help writing LookML and building reports.

item.title: Bonsai
item.description:
Bonsai bundles the paperwork of independent work. A freelancer sends a proposal, converts it into a contract with e-signature, tracks time or milestones, sends an invoice, and receives payment. A client portal keeps everything in one place, which helps a one-person business look established.

Additional tools cover running the business. Expense tracking, tax estimates, and banking features support finances, and workflow automations send reminders for unpaid invoices. AI helps draft contract language and project descriptions. Templates are available for design, consulting, development, and other fields.

item.title: Catchlight
item.description:
Catchlight is a lead scoring tool for financial advisory firms. It enriches a prospect’s profile with data such as estimated income, investable assets, age range, and interests, then applies a model trained on past conversions to produce a score showing how likely they are to become a client.

Advisors use it to prioritize their time. Instead of calling every inquiry, they can focus on those with the best fit, and see context to start a conversation. It integrates with CRMs used by advisors, such as Wealthbox, and appears in platforms that serve wealth management firms.

item.title: Meltwater
item.description:
Meltwater is a media monitoring and social listening platform. Users set up searches for brand names, competitors, and topics, and the system collects mentions from news sites, blogs, social networks, forums, and broadcast sources, with alerts and dashboards.

Analytics show volume, sentiment, and reach, and AI highlights trends and unusual spikes, such as the start of a negative story. Tools for PR teams include media databases for finding journalists, and distribution of press releases. Reports demonstrate the impact of campaigns.

item.title: Qualtrics
item.description:
Qualtrics is an experience management platform. Organizations use it to run customer satisfaction surveys, product research, brand studies, and employee engagement programs. A powerful survey builder handles complex logic, and results flow into dashboards segmented by customer, team, or time.

AI features turn feedback into action. They analyze comments for sentiment and themes, spot issues as they emerge, predict which customers may leave, and suggest next steps. The platform also pulls in data from support calls, reviews, and social media.

item.title: Relativity
item.description:
Relativity is a leading e-discovery platform. Legal teams load documents collected in a case, and the system processes them, makes them searchable, and lets reviewers tag and code them for relevance, privilege, and confidentiality. RelativityOne runs in the cloud.

AI helps lawyers cut review volume. Active learning ranks documents by likely relevance, clustering groups similar items, and generative features summarize documents and find key evidence. Analytics show patterns in communications, and audit trails support defensible processes.

item.title: ServiceTitan
item.description:
ServiceTitan is built for home service trades. Call center staff book jobs, dispatchers assign technicians, technicians use a mobile app to quote and invoice with good-better-best pricing, and the office tracks job costs, marketing, and payroll. Everything ties to one customer record.

Data and AI help companies grow. Tools score inbound calls, flag missed opportunities, recommend pricing, and predict technician performance, and agents assist with booking and follow-ups. Reporting shows revenue per technician and marketing return.

item.title: Flexport
item.description:
Flexport is a freight forwarder with a software platform. Companies that import and export goods book shipments, track containers, manage documents, and handle customs through a single interface, instead of coordinating by email with many parties. It also offers financing, warehousing, and trade services.

Technology handles repetitive work. AI reads shipping documents, checks customs data for errors, and predicts delays based on port, carrier, and weather information. An assistant answers questions about shipment status and helps with classification of goods. Data from many shipments feeds analytics on cost and performance.

item.title: Trust & Will
item.description:
Trust & Will makes estate planning approachable. A user answers questions about family, assets, and wishes, and the platform produces documents tailored to their state’s law. Plans can include wills, revocable trusts, powers of attorney, and healthcare directives.

Legal review options and notarization help make documents valid, and the service stores them securely. Price is usually lower than a full attorney engagement, which draws people who have put off planning.

item.title: Wealth.com
item.description:
Wealth.com brings estate planning into the advisory relationship. Advisors can generate estate documents for clients through guided workflows, with attorney review options, and offer a client portal that shows the plan visually. A vault stores documents.

AI reads existing estate documents and summarizes provisions, beneficiaries, and issues, which helps advisors understand a client’s situation quickly. The platform integrates with financial planning tools so estate information sits alongside the rest of the plan.

item.title: 15Five
item.description:
15Five helps organizations manage how people work and develop. Employees submit short weekly check-ins about priorities, progress, and morale, and managers review them and respond, which keeps a regular rhythm of communication. The platform includes performance reviews, goal and OKR tracking, one-on-one meeting agendas, recognition features, and engagement surveys to measure how employees feel.

AI is used to support managers. The system can summarize check-in responses and survey results, suggest coaching tips, help write review feedback, and flag potential issues like declining engagement or flight risk. Its Best-Self Management framework offers training for managers on developing teams. Reports give HR leaders a view of trends across teams.

item.title: 6sense
item.description:
6sense helps B2B teams find buyers who are not yet raising their hands. It collects signals from many sources, such as web visits, content consumption, and third-party research activity, identifies the companies behind the anonymous traffic, and uses machine learning to predict which accounts are in the market and at what stage of the buying journey. Teams see lists of target accounts ranked by readiness to buy.

The platform acts on those insights. Marketing can run advertising aimed at accounts showing interest, sales gets alerts when key accounts spike in activity, and workflows enroll contacts in email sequences. AI agents help with outreach and qualification, and integrations with CRMs and marketing automation tools keep data in sync. Predictions rely on data from many sources, so they are probabilistic.

item.title: 7shifts
item.description:
7shifts is built for the quirks of restaurant staffing. Managers create schedules based on forecast sales, availability, and labor targets, and publish them to a staff app where employees can see shifts, request swaps, and pick up open shifts. The goal is to keep enough people on the floor without overspending on wages.

The platform adds operations tools. A time clock tracks hours, compliance features flag overtime and break rules by location, tip pooling and distribution help with fair payouts, and team chat replaces scattered text threads. Integrations with point of sale systems provide sales data that feeds labor forecasts, and payroll exports reduce manual work.

item.title: Ada
item.description: Ada helps companies handle customer support questions without adding staff. Its AI agent answers inquiries on websites, in apps, and over messaging channels by drawing on a company’s knowledge base and systems, and it can take actions such as checking an order, changing an address, or processing a return by connecting to back-end tools. When a request is too complex or sensitive, it hands the conversation to a human agent with context.

item.title: ADP
item.description:
ADP is one of the best-known payroll companies in the world. It pays employees, files payroll taxes, and manages benefits administration, time and attendance, hiring, and HR records. Products range from simple small-business payroll to large, multi-country platforms for enterprises, and many companies outsource payroll entirely to ADP to ensure accuracy and compliance with changing tax rules.

Technology is increasingly part of the offering. ADP uses AI for assistants that answer HR and payroll questions, flag errors before payroll runs, and give managers insight into workforce trends, using its large dataset of payroll information to benchmark pay and turnover. The platform integrates with accounting and HR systems, and mobile apps let employees see pay stubs and request time off.

item.title: Airbyte
item.description: Airbyte solves the data movement problem. Data teams use it to pull information from applications, databases, and APIs, such as Salesforce, Postgres, Stripe, and Google Ads, and load it into destinations such as Snowflake, BigQuery, and Databricks, on a schedule. Hundreds of pre-built connectors cover common sources, and a low-code builder, with AI assistance, lets teams create connectors for others. Because it is open source, the connector catalog grows with community contributions.

item.title: AlphaSense
item.description: AlphaSense is a search engine for business information. Analysts, investors, and strategy teams use it to find what companies and experts are saying across a large body of documents: earnings call transcripts, SEC filings, broker and industry research, press releases, news, and expert call transcripts. Its search understands financial language, so a query for supply chain risk or pricing pressure returns relevant passages instead of just keyword matches, with highlights and context.

item.title: Amplitude AI
item.description: Amplitude helps product teams see what users actually do. You instrument your app or website to send events, such as signing up, clicking a button, or finishing a purchase, and Amplitude turns them into funnels, retention curves, user paths, and cohorts. These views answer questions like where new users drop off and which features bring people back. It is used by product managers, designers, and data analysts at companies from startups to large enterprises.

item.title: Apollo
item.description:
Apollo gives sales teams a place to find and contact prospects. Users search a database of people and companies by title, industry, size, and technology used, then add leads to email sequences, calling lists, and LinkedIn tasks. A browser extension finds contact details as you browse the web.

The platform includes tools for the whole outbound workflow: email verification, scheduling, a dialer, meeting booking, analytics, and integrations with CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot. AI features help write messages, score leads, and automate steps, and workflows can enrich existing records to keep a CRM current.

item.title: Apollo
item.description: Apollo is one of the most used tools for outbound sales. At its core is a searchable database of business contacts and companies, which you can filter by job title, industry, company size, location, technology used, and more. You export the matches or push them into sequences, and Apollo supplies emails and phone numbers. Startups and small sales teams like that it bundles data and outreach in one affordable product.

item.title: Attention Insight
item.description: Attention Insight offers an inexpensive shortcut to a classic design question: will anyone notice this? Upload a screenshot, ad, packaging mockup, or video, and its AI produces a heatmap of the areas likely to draw the eye in the first few seconds. The model is trained on eye-tracking data, so the predictions approximate what real viewers would do. It returns results in seconds, which makes it practical to compare several versions of a design.

item.title: Attentive
item.description:
Attentive helps brands market over text message. Shoppers opt in through signup forms and popups, and the brand sends campaigns, product alerts, and automated messages such as abandoned cart reminders and back-in-stock notices. Messages can include images and links, and customers can reply to start a conversation.

AI plays a part in targeting and content. The platform chooses send times, predicts which offers each subscriber might respond to, and helps write messages in a brand’s voice. Integrations with Shopify, Klaviyo, and other tools bring in purchase data, and analytics tie messages to revenue. A service team often helps brands set up programs.

item.title: Balto
item.description:
Balto sits beside an agent during a call. The software listens to the conversation, recognizes where it is in a script or process, and shows prompts on the agent’s screen: a question to ask, a compliance statement to read, a way to answer an objection. The aim is consistent performance across a team and less reliance on memory.

Supervisors benefit as well. Balto scores calls automatically, shows which behaviors lead to better outcomes, and reduces the number of calls reviewers must listen to by hand. New agents can ramp faster because the software coaches them in real time. Industries with strict rules, such as insurance and financial services, use it for compliance.

item.title: BambooHR
item.description:
BambooHR is built for companies without a large HR department. It keeps employee information in one place, tracks time off, handles onboarding checklists and documents, and offers an employee self-service portal. Applicant tracking helps with hiring, performance tools support reviews and goals, and payroll and benefits administration are available for U.S. customers. Reporting shows headcount, turnover, and other metrics.

The product is known for being easy to use, with a friendly interface and quick setup. AI features help HR teams with tasks such as drafting job descriptions and performance review language, summarizing feedback, and answering employee questions using company policies. Integrations connect with accounting, benefits, and productivity tools, and an app marketplace extends the platform.

item.title: Betterworks
item.description:
Betterworks supports how companies manage performance throughout the year. Employees set goals or OKRs that link to company priorities, managers hold regular check-ins, and feedback and recognition are captured along the way. Review cycles then draw on this record, so evaluations rely less on recent memory.

AI features help with the writing and analysis. An assistant can improve goal statements, summarize a year of feedback into review drafts, and suggest coaching points, while analytics show goal progress and engagement across teams. Integrations connect with HR systems like Workday and collaboration tools such as Slack and Microsoft Teams.

item.title: BigCommerce
item.description:
BigCommerce provides the pieces needed to sell online. A merchant sets up a storefront with themes, manages products and inventory, accepts payments, calculates shipping and tax, and sells across channels such as Amazon, eBay, Google, social platforms, and marketplaces. Many features that other platforms handle through apps, such as product variants, reviews, and discounts, are built in, which keeps costs more predictable.

It stands out in two areas. It supports B2B commerce with features like customer-specific pricing, quotes, and bulk ordering, and it’s designed for headless setups in which the storefront is built separately and connected through APIs, which suits brands wanting a custom front end. AI tools help generate product descriptions, support merchandising, and optimize search, and an ecosystem of apps and partners extends the platform.

item.title: BILL AI
item.description:
BILL helps businesses handle bills and payments without paper and manual entry. Vendors’ invoices arrive by email or upload, the system extracts the details, routes them for approval, and schedules payment by ACH, check, or card. On the receivables side, it sends invoices to customers and collects payments.

AI takes on the data entry. It reads invoice fields, suggests accounting categories, matches invoices to purchase orders and receipts, and flags duplicates or unusual items. Integrations with QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite, and other accounting systems keep the books in sync, and spend management tools add corporate cards and expense tracking.

item.title: Blue Yonder
item.description: Blue Yonder helps companies plan and run their supply chains. Demand forecasting predicts what customers will buy, inventory planning decides how much stock to hold and where, and transportation and warehouse systems manage how goods move. Retailers, manufacturers, and logistics providers use it to balance supply and demand, reduce stockouts and excess inventory, and respond to disruptions. The company grew from JDA Software and acquired an AI startup that gave it its name.

item.title: Botkeeper
item.description:
Botkeeper offered accounting firms a way to scale bookkeeping with automation. Its software connected to clients’ accounting systems, categorized transactions with machine learning, reconciled accounts, and prepared financial statements, with human reviewers checking the work. The aim was to let firms serve more clients with the same staff and to reduce routine data entry.

The company raised substantial funding, but it shut down after losing a large share of its revenue when major customers were acquired and changed their arrangements. It then sold its Infinite AI platform to Xendoo, a bookkeeping firm, which said it would keep the platform active and supported as its own division. The long-term roadmap is less clear, and customers had to decide whether to move.

item.title: Brandwatch
item.description:
Brandwatch is used by marketing, communications, and research teams to understand what people say online. It collects posts and mentions from social networks, news sites, forums, blogs, and reviews, and lets analysts build searches to track a brand, a competitor, a campaign, or a topic. Dashboards show volume over time, sentiment, demographics, top influencers, and emerging themes, which helps with campaign measurement, crisis monitoring, and product feedback.

AI plays a role in making sense of the data. Language models classify sentiment and topics, group conversations into themes, summarize large sets of posts, and answer questions about the findings in natural language. Image recognition finds logos in pictures posted without any text. Alerts warn teams when mentions spike, and the social management side supports publishing and responding to messages from one place.

item.title: Capacity
item.description:
Capacity aims to be a single assistant across several support functions. It connects to a company’s knowledge sources and systems, then answers questions from employees about IT, HR, and policies, and from customers about products and orders. Automated workflows can complete actions such as resetting a password or opening a ticket.

The pitch is reducing the volume of tickets that require a person. By resolving common requests automatically and escalating the rest with context, it can free staff for harder issues. Analytics show which questions come up most and where documentation is lacking.

item.title: Casetext
item.description: Casetext began as a community site where lawyers annotated and shared case law, then grew into a legal research service with tools such as a brief-checking feature called Parallel Search, which found relevant cases using natural language. It was among the first legal technology companies to build on large language models, and its CoCounsel assistant could review documents, summarize depositions, draft research memos, and help prepare contract analyses with citations to sources.

item.title: Causal
item.description:
Causal was created for finance teams that outgrew spreadsheets. Users build models from blocks that represent revenue, headcount, and costs, link them to data from accounting and CRM systems, and see results as charts and dashboards. The structure makes models easier to follow and share than a sprawling workbook.

Scenario planning is a core strength. Teams can change assumptions, such as hiring plans or pricing, and compare outcomes side by side, then present the results to executives and investors. AI features help create models from descriptions and explain changes in numbers.

item.title: CB Insights
item.description:
CB Insights tracks the innovation economy. Its database covers private companies, funding rounds, investors, acquisitions, patents, and news, and analysts and algorithms turn that into research on market trends. Corporate strategy teams, investors, and consultants use it to understand which sectors are growing and who the major players are.

Features include company profiles, market maps, forecasts of company outcomes, and an AI assistant that answers questions from the platform’s data and research. Alerts and newsletters keep subscribers up to date, and tools support building lists of companies matching specific criteria.

item.title: CharlieHR
item.description:
CharlieHR is designed for companies without a dedicated HR team. It keeps employee records, tracks time off, runs onboarding checklists, stores contracts, and supports regular reviews and one-on-ones. The interface is simple, so small teams can adopt it without lengthy setup.

An AI assistant helps with everyday HR questions about policies and employment topics, and supports tasks such as drafting job descriptions or other documents. Integrations connect with payroll providers, so data does not need to be entered twice. Reports give founders a view of headcount and absence.

item.title: Chatbase
item.description: Chatbase started as a simple way to create a chatbot from your own data. You upload files, point it to a website, or connect sources such as Notion, and it builds an agent that answers questions using that information. You embed the chat widget on your site with a snippet of code and you have support available around the clock. The simplicity made it popular with small businesses and startups that wanted a support bot without engineering work.

item.title: Chorus.ai
item.description:
Chorus records sales calls and video meetings and turns them into searchable transcripts. Managers can look through conversations to see what customers say about price, competitors, or objections, instead of relying on reps’ summaries. The tool tags topics, tracks talk time and question patterns, and highlights key moments, which makes it faster to review a call than to listen to the whole recording.

The AI layer analyzes patterns across many conversations. It can surface deals that appear to be at risk, detect competitor mentions, summarize each call, and suggest next steps. Coaching features let managers share clips, give feedback, and compare reps against top performers. Integrations with Salesforce and other CRMs send call data and notes into the customer record so reps spend less time on updates.

item.title: Clari
item.description:
Clari began as a tool to make sales forecasting more reliable. It reads CRM data and signals from email, calendar, and calls to show how deals are progressing, then rolls those into a forecast that managers can inspect by team, region, and stage. The goal is to replace spreadsheet-based forecast calls with data that people trust.

AI helps spot trouble. It scores deals, flags those with stalled activity or missing stakeholders, and suggests actions. Conversation intelligence summarizes calls and highlights risks, and pipeline inspection tools show where coverage is thin. Revenue leaders use it to prepare for board and forecast meetings.

item.title: Compass
item.description:
Compass is a brokerage that positions itself as a technology company. Its agents use a platform that combines a customer relationship manager, marketing tools for listings, market data, and transaction management in one place. Homebuyers and sellers use the site and app to search listings, see market trends, and work with an agent, and the tools are free to consumers because the company earns money through commissions on sales.

Technology supports the agent workflow. The platform helps with pricing recommendations, creates marketing materials such as brochures and social posts, tracks leads and client conversations, and organizes documents and deadlines through a deal. AI features assist with drafting listing descriptions, summarizing client interactions, and surfacing homes or clients to contact. The company has also tested private listings strategies for sellers.

item.title: Conversica
item.description:
Conversica automates the follow-up that sales teams often drop. When a lead comes in, the AI assistant sends personalized messages, reads replies, answers questions, and tries to book a meeting. If a prospect does not respond, it continues with a sequence of nudges, which keeps leads from going cold.

The assistants are used in industries such as automotive, education, software, and financial services, where large volumes of inquiries arrive. Conversation data flows into the CRM, so salespeople see which leads are qualified and what was said. The company has added generative AI to make conversations more natural.

item.title: Crimson Hexagon
item.description: Crimson Hexagon was a consumer insights company that analyzed social media, news, forums, and review data at large scale. It was known for its ForSight platform and for machine learning that classified posts by sentiment and topic with accuracy that researchers could tune. Market researchers, agencies, and brands used it to track what people said about products and campaigns, and its archive of historical social data was a draw for studying trends over time.

item.title: Crunchbase
item.description:
Crunchbase is a widely used database about startups and private companies. Users look up a company to see its founders, funding history, investors, and news, or search for companies by industry, location, and stage. Investors, salespeople, and researchers use it to find targets and track activity.

Predictive features add forward-looking signals. AI models estimate which companies are likely to raise money, grow, or be acquired, and alerts notify users when relevant events happen. Lists and integrations send data into CRMs for prospecting.

item.title: Culture Amp
item.description:
Culture Amp helps companies listen to employees. HR teams run engagement, onboarding, and exit surveys, analyze the results by team and demographic group, and compare against benchmarks from other organizations. Dashboards point out areas where scores are low and what drives them.

The platform also covers performance and development, with review cycles, goal tracking, and feedback. AI helps by summarizing open-ended comments into themes, drafting review text, and recommending actions to managers, which saves analysts days of reading. An assistant answers questions about results.

item.title: DataRobot
item.description:
DataRobot pioneered automated machine learning. A data team uploads a dataset, and the platform tries many algorithms and feature combinations, ranks them, and explains the best models, which lowers the barrier to building predictive models for tasks such as churn, demand, and risk. It also handles deployment and monitoring, tracking model accuracy and drift once models are live.

The company has pivoted toward generative AI and agents. Its platform now helps companies build and run AI agents and applications, with governance features such as documentation, bias checks, approvals, and audit trails that matter in industries such as banking, insurance, and healthcare. It can run in the cloud or on a company’s own infrastructure and integrates with major cloud providers and data platforms.

item.title: dbt Cloud
item.description:
dbt, short for data build tool, became the standard way to transform raw data inside a warehouse such as Snowflake, BigQuery, or Databricks. Analysts write SQL select statements, define dependencies among them, and dbt builds tables and views in the right order, with version control, testing, and documentation. This brings software engineering practices like code review and continuous integration to analytics work.

dbt Cloud is the hosted product from dbt Labs. It provides a browser-based IDE, job scheduling, CI that tests changes before they reach production, a data catalog with lineage, and a semantic layer that defines metrics once for use across BI tools. AI features help generate models, tests, and documentation, and answer questions about the project, which speeds up repetitive tasks.

item.title: Demandbase
item.description:
Demandbase focuses on selling to companies rather than individuals. It builds a view of target accounts from first-party and third-party data, including website visits, content use, and intent signals showing which accounts are researching a topic. Marketing and sales teams see which accounts are heating up and who within them is involved.

The platform acts on those signals. Advertising features serve targeted ads to the buying committee at chosen accounts, sales tools alert reps when accounts show interest, and orchestration coordinates campaigns across channels. AI helps score accounts, predict fit, and recommend actions, and an assistant answers questions about account data.

item.title: DocuSign AI
item.description:
Docusign made electronic signatures routine. Senders upload a document, specify signers and fields, and recipients sign on any device, with an audit trail and legal validity in many countries. It’s used for sales contracts, HR paperwork, real estate, and any agreement that once needed a pen, and it integrates with Salesforce, Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, and many business systems.

The company has expanded to manage the whole agreement lifecycle. Its Intelligent Agreement Management platform includes tools to prepare and negotiate agreements, a repository that stores them, and AI that reads contracts to extract terms such as renewal dates, obligations, and parties. Its AI can summarize documents, answer questions about a contract portfolio, and flag risks, and workflow tools automate steps such as approvals and routing.

item.title: Domo AI
item.description:
Domo aims to put an organization’s data in one place. It connects to hundreds of sources, from databases and spreadsheets to marketing and finance platforms, and lets users clean and combine data and then build dashboards and reports. Business users can view metrics on the web or mobile and set alerts, and developers can build custom apps on top of the data.

AI is built through the product. Users can ask questions in natural language and receive charts and answers, models can forecast and detect anomalies, and AI agents and workflows can automate tasks, such as summarizing reports or triggering actions when numbers change. Domo also lets companies connect their own models, and offers governance features for data access.

item.title: DoNotPay
item.description:
DoNotPay started by helping people contest parking tickets and grew into an app for dealing with the small annoyances of consumer life. Its tools help users write letters and fill out forms to dispute charges, cancel unwanted subscriptions, request refunds, and complain to companies and agencies. The idea is that many of these tasks are tedious and intimidating, and a template-driven assistant can save people time and money.

The company’s marketing as the world’s first robot lawyer caused trouble. The Federal Trade Commission alleged that the service did not perform as well as a human lawyer and did not have the testing to back its claims. A final order barred DoNotPay from making that kind of claim without evidence and required it to pay a fine and notify affected customers. The case is often cited as a warning about overstating what AI can do in legal matters.

item.title: Dynamic Yield
item.description:
Dynamic Yield helps businesses show each customer the content most likely to interest them. It collects behavior data from web, mobile, and email channels, builds profiles and segments, and uses machine learning to choose which products, banners, or messages to show. Retailers use it for recommendations like customers also bought, personalized homepages, and tailored promotions.

The platform also covers testing and optimization. Teams run experiments to compare versions of pages, with statistics to determine winners, and use triggers such as exit intent to present timely offers. Integrations connect with e-commerce platforms, customer data platforms, and marketing tools, and AI features suggest audiences and automate decisions. It supports use in industries including retail, travel, banking, and media.

item.title: Expensify
item.description:
Expensify is known for making expense reports less painful. Employees photograph receipts or forward them by email, SmartScan extracts the merchant, date, and amount, and the app builds a report for submission. Managers approve in the app, and approved expenses sync to accounting software.

Other features cover company spending. The Expensify Card gives employees corporate cards with real-time receipts matching, policies flag out-of-bounds expenses automatically, and mileage tracking and per diems handle travel. AI helps categorize spending and spot policy issues.

item.title: Factorial
item.description:
Factorial gathers HR tasks in one system. Companies store employee records, track attendance and time off, manage documents and contracts, run performance reviews, and handle recruiting and onboarding. Payroll is offered in several countries, and integrations connect with accounting and communication tools.

AI helps with administrative work. It can draft job descriptions and offer letters, answer employee questions about policies, and speed up payroll preparation. Reports give managers a view of headcount and absence.

item.title: Fivetran
item.description:
Fivetran handles the extract and load steps of data pipelines. A team connects sources such as SaaS applications, databases, and files, picks a destination warehouse, and Fivetran keeps the data synced, adapting automatically when source schemas change. This saves engineers from building and maintaining custom connectors.

The company merged with dbt Labs, the maker of the popular transformation tool, bringing loading and transformation together under one roof. Related products include a metadata and governance layer, and tools that prepare data for AI agents. Features for monitoring, anomaly detection, and lineage help teams trust their data.

item.title: Forethought AI
item.description: Forethought applies AI to the work that fills support queues. It reads incoming tickets and classifies them by topic and urgency, routes them to the right team, and drafts answers for human agents using the company’s knowledge base and past tickets. For common questions, its AI agents answer directly in chat and email and take simple actions such as checking an order status, handing off to a person when they cannot resolve the issue.

item.title: Freshdesk
item.description: Freshdesk gives support teams a single place to handle customer requests. Messages from email, a web form, live chat, phone, and channels like WhatsApp, Messenger, and Instagram land in a shared inbox as tickets that can be assigned, tagged, prioritized, and tracked against service-level targets. A knowledge base lets customers find answers on their own, and a customer portal shows the status of their requests. It is used by companies from small startups to large support organizations.

item.title: Gladly
item.description:
Gladly organizes support around the customer, not the ticket. Instead of separate cases for each channel, all interactions with a person appear in a single timeline, so an agent sees the entire history when a customer reaches out. That makes support feel more personal and reduces repeating information.

Sidekick is the AI part. It answers common questions, completes tasks like order lookups, and hands off to a human with context when needed. Assistive features summarize history and suggest replies. Gladly is used by consumer brands that care about the quality of service.

item.title: Gong
item.description:
Gong captures sales conversations and turns them into insight. It records calls and meetings, transcribes them, and pulls in emails and CRM data, then analyzes what is happening across the pipeline: which topics come up in deals that close, how often competitors are mentioned, how much reps talk compared with customers, and where deals are stalling. Managers can search a library of calls instead of relying on reps’ summaries.

The AI features save time at several levels. Calls are summarized with key points and next steps, which are written back to the CRM. Deal boards highlight risks, such as no recent contact with a decision-maker, and forecasting tools estimate which deals will close. Coaching tools find moments to review and compare behavior across reps, and newer AI agents help with tasks such as preparing for meetings, researching accounts, and drafting follow-ups.

item.title: Gorgias
item.description:
Gorgias is a helpdesk made for online stores. Messages from email, live chat, social media, SMS, and phone arrive in one inbox, with the customer’s order history, shipping status, and account details shown next to the conversation. Agents can refund an order, edit an address, or cancel a shipment without leaving the ticket, which speeds up the most common support tasks in retail.

Automation takes care of a lot of the repetitive work. Rules route and tag tickets, macros fill in standard replies with order data, and self-service flows let shoppers track orders or request returns. An AI agent answers questions about shipping, returns, and products using the store’s policies and catalog, and can complete actions in the store before passing complex issues to people. Gorgias can also support sales conversations and product recommendations.

item.title: Greenhouse
item.description: Greenhouse is an applicant tracking system for companies that want hiring to be systematic instead of ad hoc. Each job has a defined process: a posting, a set of stages, interview kits with questions, and scorecards that interviewers fill out against the same criteria. The aim is to reduce bias and gut-feel decisions by making every candidate go through the same structured steps. Recruiters, hiring managers, and interviewers each get a view suited to their part of the work.

item.title: H2O.ai
item.description:
H2O.ai built its reputation on open-source machine learning. H2O-3 is a widely used library for training models on large datasets, with an AutoML feature that tries many algorithms and picks the best. The company’s commercial Driverless AI automated feature engineering and model building for business users, and its tools have been used in finance, insurance, and healthcare.

More recently, H2O.ai has focused on generative AI. H2O LLM Studio lets teams fine-tune language models without much code, h2oGPT is an open-source project for chatting with documents, and its enterprise platform lets companies deploy private assistants and agents, including on-premises or in air-gapped environments. It has also released small language models designed to run efficiently.

item.title: Harvey
item.description:
Harvey was built for lawyers and has become one of the best-known legal AI companies. Attorneys use its assistant to ask legal questions, draft and revise contracts and memos, summarize documents, and analyze large sets of files, such as the documents in a due diligence review. It runs on leading language models adapted for legal work and is designed to provide citations so lawyers can verify the answers.

Beyond a chat assistant, Harvey offers structured features. Vault stores and analyzes large document collections, workflows automate multi-step tasks such as contract review against a playbook, and integrations connect with tools law firms already use, including document management and legal research providers. Firms can customize the system with their own templates and precedents, and security controls support the confidentiality requirements of legal practice.

item.title: Helpshift
item.description:
Helpshift places support inside the app. Users reach help from a screen in a game or mobile product, without leaving to email, and conversations carry context about the device, account, and recent activity. Agents see this information and respond in the same thread.

AI reduces the load. Intent detection reads messages, classifies the issue, and routes it to the right team, while chatbots answer common questions and collect details before a human steps in. A knowledge base and automation tools support self-service, and analytics track satisfaction and resolution times.

item.title: HiBob
item.description:
HiBob is built for companies that want a modern HR system for distributed teams. It stores employee records, handles onboarding and time off, supports performance reviews, and manages compensation and benefits. The interface is designed for employees as well as HR, with a social feel and company-wide features.

Analytics and AI help leaders. Compensation benchmarking compares pay with market data, workforce planning tools model headcount, and an assistant answers HR questions and drafts documents. Payroll integrations and a marketplace of apps connect Bob with finance and IT systems.

item.title: Hotjar AI
item.description:
Hotjar helps teams see what visitors actually do on a site. Heatmaps show where people click, move, and scroll, session recordings replay individual visits, and on-page surveys and feedback widgets ask visitors what they think. Together they reveal confusing layouts, broken elements, and places where people give up, which complements numbers from analytics tools that show what happened but not why.

AI cuts down the time it takes to find insights. Instead of watching hundreds of recordings, teams can get automatic summaries of sessions, highlights of common frustrations, and analysis of open-ended survey responses grouped into themes. This helps designers, product managers, and marketers decide what to fix first. Funnels and trends let you see where users drop out, and integrations send findings to tools like Slack, Jira, and HubSpot.

item.title: HubSpot
item.description: HubSpot started as a marketing software company and grew into a full platform for managing the customer relationship from first visit to renewal. It is organized into hubs: Marketing Hub for email, forms, ads, and landing pages, Sales Hub for pipelines and sequences, Service Hub for tickets and help desk, Content Hub for websites and blogs, and Operations Hub for data syncing and automation. All of them read from the same CRM, so a marketer, a sales rep, and a support agent are looking at one record of the customer.

item.title: HubSpot
item.description: HubSpot began as an inbound marketing tool, and Marketing Hub is still the center of its original idea: attract visitors with useful content, capture them as contacts, and nurture them toward a purchase. It includes email marketing, landing pages, forms, blogging, social publishing, ad tracking, and SEO recommendations, all tied to a CRM that records every interaction with a contact. That shared data is what lets a marketer see which campaigns produce actual customers, not only clicks.

item.title: HubSpot CRM
item.description: HubSpot CRM is the shared database underneath every HubSpot product, and it can also be used on its own at no cost. It stores contacts, companies, deals, and tickets, logs emails and calls against each record, and shows a pipeline of deals by stage. Connecting Gmail or Outlook means sent and received messages are attached to the right contact automatically, so people spend less time on manual data entry. For a small business that has been running on spreadsheets, it is an easy first step into a real CRM.

item.title: Hunter
item.description: Hunter is a tool for finding contact details for business outreach. A Domain Search shows the email addresses associated with a company along with the sources where they were found, and the email pattern the company uses. An Email Finder takes a person’s name and company and returns the most likely address with a confidence score. Email Verifier checks whether an address is valid and likely to deliver, which reduces bounces.

item.title: Intercom
item.description:
Intercom began as a live chat widget for websites and now covers the full range of customer communication. It combines a messenger on your site or app, a shared inbox for support teams, a searchable help center, email, and product tours. Companies use it to answer questions, onboard new users, and keep conversations in one thread across channels. It is common among software and subscription businesses.

Fin is the AI agent at the center of the current product. It reads your help articles and past conversations, then answers customer questions directly in chat and email, including follow-ups. When it cannot solve a problem or the customer asks for a person, it hands the conversation to a human with context attached. Fin can also take actions in other systems, like checking an order or updating an account, if you connect it. A copilot for human agents drafts replies and summarizes long threads.

item.title: Ironclad
item.description:
Ironclad serves legal and business teams that handle many contracts. Requests start from templates through a workflow, drafts are negotiated with counterparties inside the platform, and approvals and e-signatures finish the process. Executed contracts become structured data in a repository.

AI features are central. They read incoming contracts, flag deviations from company positions, suggest edits, and extract key terms such as renewal dates and liability caps. A repository search lets teams answer questions about their agreements, and reports show where contracts get stuck.

item.title: Jasper
item.description:
As a marketing platform, Jasper aims to speed up the full path from a brief to a finished campaign. Marketers define their brand voice, audience, and product information once, then generate blog posts, social posts, ads, emails, and landing pages that follow those guidelines. Campaign tools help plan content around a launch, adapt messages for each channel, and keep versions organized.

The latest versions emphasize agents and workflows. Specialized agents handle tasks such as researching a topic, creating a content calendar, repurposing a webinar into several assets, and optimizing copy for search. Integrations connect with tools such as Google Docs, Webflow, and HubSpot, and analytics features tie content to performance. Controls let enterprises govern who can use what and ensure compliance with brand rules.

item.title: Juro
item.description:
Juro puts the contract workflow in a browser editor. Sales and business teams generate contracts from approved templates, negotiate with counterparties in the same document, collect signatures, and store the result in a searchable repository. Legal sets the rules and approvals, so routine deals move without a lawyer.

AI is part of the product. It can draft clauses from a plain-English description, review third-party paper against a company’s positions, summarize agreements, and answer questions about the contract portfolio. Integrations with CRMs and messaging tools keep the process connected to sales.

item.title: Kensho
item.description:
Kensho began as a startup applying machine learning to financial markets and was acquired by S&P Global, where it operates as the company’s AI innovation hub. Its products address practical data problems in finance. Kensho Link matches records between data sets, such as linking company names across different sources, Kensho Classify tags documents by category, and Kensho Extract pulls data out of PDFs and filings.

More recent work connects financial data to generative AI. Kensho develops tools that allow AI assistants and agents to access S&P Global’s data reliably, with grounding that provides sources for answers, plus language models and benchmarks for finance. Its technology supports S&P products and is available to clients who want to build their own applications.

item.title: Kira Systems
item.description:
Kira was one of the first widely adopted machine learning tools in legal work. It reads contracts and identifies provisions such as change of control, termination rights, assignment, and indemnification, then extracts the relevant text into a structured summary. Lawyers use it in mergers and acquisitions due diligence, where hundreds or thousands of agreements must be reviewed quickly, and in lease, finance, and compliance reviews.

Litera acquired Kira Systems and continues to develop it. The newer version adds generative AI to the original extraction models, with features like rapid clause analysis that organizes clauses across many documents. Users can start from built-in models for common provisions, train their own for specific needs, and review results in a side-by-side view that links back to the source text. Integration with Litera’s other tools connects review to drafting and transaction workflows.

item.title: Kustomer AI
item.description:
Kustomer takes a CRM-style approach to support. Instead of treating each ticket as an isolated item, it builds a timeline for each customer that includes every conversation, order, and interaction across channels. Agents see the full history in one view, which reduces the need to ask customers to repeat themselves. Channels include email, chat, SMS, social messaging, and voice, and workflow rules automate routing and tagging.

AI features have grown in importance. AI agents can answer common questions, check order status, and complete simple actions, escalating complex cases to humans with context. Tools for human agents summarize long histories, suggest replies, and classify issues, and insights analyze conversation patterns to find problems in products or processes. The system connects with e-commerce and business platforms to bring in order and account data.

item.title: Lattice AI
item.description:
Lattice helps companies run performance and development programs. Managers and employees complete reviews and give continuous feedback, set goals and OKRs, hold one-on-ones with shared agendas, and track growth plans. Engagement surveys measure how employees feel, and compensation tools support pay reviews and planning, while an HR information system keeps employee records.

AI is added to reduce busywork. It can help managers draft feedback and review summaries, analyze survey comments for themes, and suggest talking points for one-on-ones. Insights flag possible retention risks or teams with low engagement, and an AI assistant answers questions about company data. The company has also launched products for managing AI agents as part of the workforce, a controversial idea.

item.title: LawGeex
item.description:
LawGeex addresses the high volume of routine contracts that reach legal departments, such as NDAs and standard vendor agreements. Legal teams define a playbook that states what is acceptable in each type of clause, and LawGeex’s AI reads incoming contracts and checks them against it. Contracts that conform can be approved quickly, and those that deviate are flagged with the problem and suggested edits.

The idea is to let lawyers focus on contracts that really need judgment. Business users can submit documents for review through integrations and workflows, and reviewers see a clear summary of what matched, what did not, and where to look. The system learns from corrections, and reporting shows how many contracts were reviewed and how long approvals take. It supports a range of commercial agreements.

item.title: Leapsome
item.description:
Leapsome gathers people processes in one product. HR teams run review cycles, set goals and OKRs, send engagement surveys, deliver learning content, and manage compensation planning, with the data connected so decisions draw on the full picture. It is used by mid-sized, often distributed companies.

AI helps with the heaviest reading and writing. It summarizes feedback, analyzes comments from surveys for sentiment and themes, helps managers draft reviews, and suggests development actions. Dashboards show trends by team.

item.title: Lexion
item.description:
Lexion helped legal teams make sense of their contracts. It read agreements, pulled out terms like parties, dates, renewal windows, and liability caps, and stored them in a searchable repository. Alerts warned teams about upcoming renewals and obligations, and workflows routed new requests.

AI answered questions across the portfolio, such as which contracts have auto-renewal or a particular clause. The company was built for fast-growing technology companies that wanted contract management without a heavy implementation.

item.title: LinkedIn Sales Navigator
item.description:
Sales Navigator gives salespeople deeper access to LinkedIn’s network. It provides advanced filters for finding people and companies, such as by seniority, function, company size, industry, and recent job changes. Users save leads and accounts into lists, and the system sends alerts when something relevant happens, like a prospect changing jobs or a company hiring in a certain department, which can prompt a timely message.

Further features support outreach. InMail messages reach people outside your network, TeamLink shows how colleagues are connected to a prospect for warm introductions, and integrations sync with CRMs such as Salesforce and HubSpot to keep records current. AI tools recommend leads, summarize accounts, and suggest ways to start a conversation, using the profile and activity data on the platform.

item.title: Llamasoft
item.description:
Llamasoft helped companies answer strategic supply chain questions. Where should factories and warehouses be placed? How would costs change if a port closes or demand shifts? Its software builds a digital model of a supply network, then uses optimization and simulation to test alternatives and recommend the best configuration, balancing cost, service levels, and risk. Large manufacturers, retailers, and consumer goods companies used it for network design and planning.

Coupa acquired Llamasoft and folded it into its business spend management platform, so customers can connect supply chain decisions with procurement and spend data. The technology continues under Coupa branding, with capabilities such as network optimization, inventory and sourcing analysis, and demand sensing, supported by machine learning and a digital twin of the supply chain.

item.title: Luminance
item.description:
Luminance is built for lawyers who deal with large volumes of agreements. Teams upload contracts, and the platform identifies key terms, highlights unusual or risky clauses, and compares documents against company standards. Its origins lie in machine learning developed at the University of Cambridge.

Beyond review, Luminance supports negotiation and drafting. An AI assistant can propose edits in Word, summarize positions, and handle routine agreements with limited human involvement, escalating exceptions to lawyers. In due diligence, it speeds through thousands of documents to find issues across a deal’s data room.

item.title: Magento
item.description:
Magento was created as an open-source e-commerce framework and became one of the most customizable platforms for online stores. Merchants with complex needs use it to manage large catalogs, multiple storefronts and currencies, custom pricing and checkout, and integrations with ERP and other systems. A huge ecosystem of extensions, agencies, and developers supports it.

Adobe acquired Magento and sells a commercial version, Adobe Commerce, with additional features for B2B selling, merchandising, and cloud hosting and support, plus integration with Adobe’s marketing and analytics products. Adobe Sensei AI powers features such as product recommendations and search. The free Magento Open Source edition continues for those who want to host and manage their own stores.

item.title: MarketMan
item.description:
MarketMan is back-of-house software for food service. Operators record what they buy and use, build recipes with ingredient costs, and see the cost of each dish. When prices change or usage varies, the system flags it, helping managers protect margins.

Ordering and invoicing are handled in one place. Staff place orders with suppliers, receive deliveries, and match invoices to what arrived, which catches errors and short shipments. Forecasting tools predict how much to order based on sales history, and integrations connect with point of sale and accounting systems.

item.title: MarketMuse
item.description:
MarketMuse approaches content from the perspective of topical authority. It scans your website and compares the topics you cover with what search engines expect from a site in your area, then shows gaps where new or improved content could help. Instead of focusing on single keywords, it helps plan clusters of related articles that together establish expertise.

Its tools turn that strategy into work. Content briefs list the subtopics, questions, and terms a piece should address, an optimization tool scores drafts against those expectations, and AI helps with drafting and updating existing pages. Metrics such as personalized difficulty estimate how hard a topic will be for your site specifically. Teams use the platform to prioritize where to invest effort.

item.title: Maze
item.description:
Maze helps product teams learn from users. Designers import a prototype from Figma, set tasks for participants, and share a link to run a test that records clicks, paths, and success rates. Surveys, card sorts, and interview studies are supported as well, and a panel service can recruit participants.

AI speeds up analysis. It transcribes sessions, pulls out themes and quotes, and writes summaries of what the data shows, so teams spend less time sorting through recordings. Reports can be shared with stakeholders.

item.title: Metabase
item.description:
Metabase makes data approachable. Connected to a database or warehouse, it lets non-technical users build questions by clicking through filters and summaries, view results as charts, and assemble dashboards. Analysts can write SQL when they need it, and everything is shareable.

The AI assistant lets users describe what they want, and generates the query or chart, which helps people who do not know the data model. Embedded analytics lets companies place dashboards in their own products. Permissions and models keep data governed.

item.title: Morningstar AI
item.description:
Morningstar is known for independent research on funds, stocks, and markets. Its star ratings for mutual funds and ETFs became a standard reference, and analysts publish research and fair value estimates on companies. Individual investors use its website and premium subscriptions to screen investments and build portfolios, while advisors and institutions use products like Morningstar Direct for deeper analysis, portfolio construction, and reporting.

AI has been added to make research easier to navigate. Mo is a conversational assistant that answers investing questions using Morningstar’s research and data, summarizes reports, and explains concepts, with an emphasis on drawing from the company’s own vetted content to limit errors. Other uses include automated summaries of earnings calls and analyst notes, and data tools that help build screens and analyze holdings.

item.title: Mosaic
item.description:
Mosaic is aimed at finance teams that want a modern view of the business. It pulls data from accounting systems, sales tools, and HR platforms into a single model, so metrics like revenue, headcount, and cash are current and consistent. Teams build reports and board decks from live data.

Forecasting and scenario tools let teams test assumptions, such as hiring plans or pricing changes, and see the impact. AI allows users to ask questions in plain language and get analysis, and automates routine commentary and variance explanations.

item.title: Netomi
item.description:
Netomi builds AI agents for customer support. Large brands connect it to their help desks and back-end systems, and the agents answer questions, track orders, process returns, and handle other requests across channels. Where an agent cannot resolve something, it hands off to a person with context.

The platform learns from past tickets and company content, and is built with controls such as guardrails and testing for regulated and high-volume environments. Customers include airlines, retailers, and travel companies that field heavy, repetitive inquiries.

item.title: Nosto
item.description:
Nosto helps online stores treat every visitor differently. It tracks browsing and purchase behavior and uses it to recommend products, order category pages, personalize search, and show targeted messages. Merchants configure these experiences with a visual tool and rules, and the system learns what works.

Features include product recommendations across the site and in emails, a search engine that understands intent, and tools to personalize content by audience. Shopify, Magento, and other platforms are supported. Generative AI helps write product copy and campaign content.

item.title: Observe.AI
item.description:
Observe.AI is built for contact centers that handle huge numbers of customer interactions. Quality teams traditionally review a small sample of calls by hand. Observe.AI transcribes and scores all interactions automatically against a company’s quality and compliance criteria, flags issues such as missed disclosures or poor handling of angry customers, and surfaces trends across thousands of conversations.

It also supports agents during and after the call. Real-time guidance suggests what to say or reminds an agent of a required step, and post-call summaries cut the time spent on notes. Coaching tools turn scores into specific feedback for each agent, and dashboards help supervisors see which skills to work on. The platform has added AI agents that speak with customers directly for routine requests, handing off to humans when needed.

item.title: Okendo
item.description:
Okendo helps online stores build trust with reviews. After a purchase, it asks customers for reviews with photos and video, displays them on product pages, and syndicates them to Google. Surveys and attributes gather more detail about the customer and product fit.

Additional tools include a loyalty and referral program and a customer data layer. AI summarizes reviews into themes, analyzes sentiment, and suggests replies, helping merchants learn what customers like and dislike. Integrations connect with email, helpdesk, and ads tools.

item.title: Opendoor
item.description:
Opendoor popularized the iBuyer model. A homeowner enters an address and details, receives an offer within days based on the company’s pricing model and an inspection, and can close on a timeline they choose. The company then repairs and resells the home. The process appeals to sellers who value speed and certainty over getting the highest price.

Technology is central to the business. Machine learning models estimate what a home is worth and how long it will take to sell, using data on the property and the local market, and these estimates determine offers and risk. Opendoor also offers listing options for sellers who prefer to sell traditionally, along with buyer services such as touring homes with self-guided access in some markets.

item.title: Oracle SCM
item.description:
Oracle SCM Cloud brings the functions of a supply chain together in one cloud application suite.
