It covers planning demand and supply, buying from suppliers, managing inventory and warehouses, running manufacturing, handling orders and fulfillment, and moving goods through transportation and global trade, with product lifecycle management for design data. Because it shares data with Oracle’s finance and HR applications, companies can connect supply chain decisions to financial outcomes.

AI and analytics support the suite. Machine learning improves demand forecasts and supply plans, predictive models flag delays and quality risks, and generative AI assistants help users find information and complete tasks. Oracle has been adding AI agents that can handle routine actions across processes. The suite is delivered in the cloud and updated regularly.

item.title: Outreach
item.description:
Outreach is used by sales teams to run structured prospecting and follow-up at scale. Reps enroll leads in sequences that combine emails, calls, LinkedIn steps, and tasks, and the platform schedules each step, tracks replies, and logs activity to the CRM. Managers can see which messages and cadences perform best, and automated rules route leads and keep work organized.

Over time, Outreach has added revenue intelligence and AI. Conversation intelligence records and analyzes calls, deal health scoring flags risk, and forecasting tools combine activity and pipeline data to estimate outcomes. AI assistants summarize meetings, draft emails, suggest next steps, and increasingly act as agents that research accounts or manage parts of the pipeline.

item.title: PandaDoc AI
item.description:
PandaDoc helps sales teams close deals faster. Users build proposals and quotes from templates in a drag-and-drop editor, add pricing tables with live calculations, embed videos and payment links, and send them to clients, who can review and sign electronically. Tracking shows when a document is opened and viewed, so reps know when to follow up.

Automation and integration make it practical for teams. It connects with CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot to populate documents with deal data and update records when documents are signed, offers approval workflows, content libraries, and a payment step. AI features help generate document content from a prompt, summarize contracts, suggest edits, and extract information, speeding up proposal creation.

item.title: People.ai
item.description:
People.ai solves the data entry problem in sales. Instead of relying on reps to log everything, it connects to email, calendars, and phone systems and records contacts, meetings, and conversations, then matches them to the right accounts and opportunities in the CRM. That keeps records current and gives managers a more complete picture of how engaged each deal is.

On top of the data, it provides analytics and AI. Dashboards show activity, engagement with key contacts, and whether deals are at risk, and forecasting tools estimate which will close. AI agents can summarize accounts, answer questions about the pipeline in natural language, and prepare reps for meetings. The aim is to give sales leaders a reliable view without chasing updates.

item.title: Persado
item.description:
Persado focuses on the specific words in marketing messages. Its premise is that the choice of language, including emotions, calls to action, and phrasing, affects whether people respond, and that machine learning can learn what works. Marketers give it a campaign goal and brand guidelines, and it generates message variations and predicts which will perform best, based on its library of language and results from past campaigns.

Large brands in finance, retail, and telecommunications use Persado to optimize email subject lines, ads, and push notifications at scale. It integrates with marketing platforms, tests variants, and learns from the results to improve future messages. More recently, the company has added generative AI tools for drafting and personalizing content within brand guardrails.

item.title: Personio
item.description:
Personio centralizes HR work. Companies keep employee data, manage leave and attendance, handle recruiting from job posting to offer, prepare payroll, and run reviews, in one system designed around European employment rules. Self-service features let employees update their own data and request time off.

AI features help with common tasks. They draft job descriptions, assist with screening candidates, answer HR questions from company policy, and automate workflows. Reports show headcount, turnover, and other metrics.

item.title: Pilot
item.description:
Pilot offers accounting as a service. A company connects its bank accounts and tools, and Pilot’s team and software keep the books, close each month, prepare financial statements, and handle tax filings. Clients get a dedicated bookkeeper and a dashboard.

Automation takes on the repetitive work, such as categorizing transactions, while humans check results and answer questions. Add-on services include CFO advice, R&D tax credits, and sales tax support.

Pilot is priced by monthly fee based on complexity, and aimed at startups and small to mid-sized businesses. It is a service, not self-serve software. Alternatives include Bench (which shut down and was acquired by Employer.com), Puzzle, Digits, Xero with an accountant, and QuickBooks Live. Pilot suits startups that want outsourced accounting.

item.title: Pipedrive
item.description: Pipedrive is designed by and for salespeople, with the pipeline at the center. Deals appear as cards that move across stages, from first contact to closed, so reps can see at a glance what needs attention. Each deal has activities, emails, notes, and files attached, and the system reminds you of follow-ups so nothing slips. Compared with big CRM suites, the interface is clean and quick to learn, which suits small and growing sales teams.

item.title: PitchBook
item.description:
PitchBook tracks private markets. Its database covers companies, funding rounds, investors, funds, acquisitions, and valuations, and analysts use it to find targets, benchmark deals, and research sectors. Reports and data feeds support investment decisions and strategy work.

AI tools help users query the database in natural language, summarize companies and markets, and speed up research tasks. Integrations with Excel and CRM systems bring data into daily workflows. The company also publishes market research.

item.title: Plaid
item.description: Plaid connects apps to bank accounts. When you link an account in a budgeting app, investment platform, or payments service, Plaid’s interface asks you to sign in to your bank, and the app then receives only the data you permit. Developers use Plaid’s APIs to verify account ownership, check balances, read transaction history, confirm identity, assess income and assets for lending, and initiate transfers, without building separate integrations with thousands of banks.

item.title: PostHog AI
item.description:
PostHog bundles the tools product teams use to understand and improve their software. After adding its SDK, you can track events, build funnels and retention charts, watch session recordings, run experiments, release features gradually with flags, collect feedback through surveys, and analyze data with SQL. Having these in one product, with a shared data set, avoids the cost and complexity of stitching several tools together.

AI features include an assistant that can answer questions about your data, write queries, create charts, and summarize insights in plain language, and tools for monitoring AI applications such as tracing model calls and costs. Because PostHog is open source, it can be self-hosted for data control, or used through PostHog Cloud, and a pipeline can send data to other destinations.

item.title: Power BI
item.description: Power BI turns raw data into visual reports. You connect to sources such as Excel files, SQL databases, cloud services, and Microsoft Fabric, shape the data, define relationships and calculations, and build dashboards with charts, maps, and slicers. Reports can be published to the Power BI service, shared with colleagues, refreshed on a schedule, and embedded in other applications. Because it fits neatly with Excel, Teams, SharePoint, and Azure, it is the default BI tool for many Microsoft-centered companies.

item.title: Privy
item.description:
Privy gives small stores a way to capture and convert visitors. Pop-ups and banners collect emails and texts with offers, automated emails recover abandoned carts, and campaigns promote products to subscribers. Everything runs from one dashboard connected to the store.

AI assists with writing and targeting, such as drafting emails and choosing segments. Templates and recipes simplify setup for merchants without a marketing team, and analytics show revenue from each campaign.

item.title: Proposify
item.description:
Proposify helps agencies and service companies create and send proposals. Teams build templates with sections, pricing tables, and brand styling, assemble a proposal quickly, and send it to clients who can review, comment, and sign electronically. Notifications show when a proposal is opened.

AI features help with writing content and suggest improvements based on what has worked in past proposals. Analytics reveal how long clients spend on each section, informing follow-ups. Integrations connect with CRMs and billing.

item.title: Qwilr
item.description:
Qwilr replaces static PDF proposals with web pages. A seller builds a proposal from blocks, such as text, images, videos, pricing tables, and acceptance sections, and sends a link. Buyers can adjust options in a pricing table, and sign online, which shortens the path to closing.

Analytics show who viewed the page, how long they spent on each section, and when they came back, which guides follow-up. Templates keep branding consistent, and integrations push data into CRMs. AI drafts content from notes and suggests improvements.

item.title: Recharge
item.description:
Recharge enables subscribe-and-save models for online stores. Merchants on Shopify and other platforms set up subscription products, let customers manage deliveries and payments in a portal, and bill on schedule. It is common in consumables such as food, supplements, and beauty products.

Analytics show retention, churn, and revenue, and tools help reduce cancellations. Smart payment retries recover failed charges, and AI models predict which subscribers may leave so merchants can intervene with offers or pauses.

item.title: Redfin
item.description:
Redfin helped modernize home search. Its site and app show listings with details, photos, and maps, along with estimated home values, price history, and tools to compare neighborhoods. A key difference from traditional brokerages is that its agents are salaried employees instead of paid mostly on commission, and Redfin has competed on lower listing fees and a customer-focused model.

Technology plays a large role. Its valuation model, the Redfin Estimate, uses machine learning on recent sales and listing data to estimate home values, and tools offer alerts, tours scheduling, and offers online. AI features help with search and recommendations. Rocket Companies, the owner of Rocket Mortgage, acquired Redfin, bringing mortgage and agent services together under a combined offering, including financing incentives when buyers use both.

item.title: Rippling
item.description:
Rippling combines employee data with the systems that depend on it. When a person joins, Rippling creates their payroll record, sets up benefits, provisions laptops and software accounts, and orders equipment, using one source of truth. Changes in the employee record cascade across the systems.

Modules cover HR, payroll in many countries, time and attendance, benefits, device and app management, and corporate cards and expenses. A workflow engine lets admins automate approvals and tasks, and AI assistants answer questions and draft content.

item.title: Salesforce
item.description: Salesforce is the CRM that large companies tend to run their sales and customer operations on. It tracks leads, accounts, opportunities, and support cases, and it is sold as separate clouds for Sales, Service, Marketing, and Commerce, with Slack, Tableau, and MuleSoft added for collaboration, analytics, and integration. Underneath is a platform that lets companies build custom objects, workflows, and apps, which is why Salesforce setups can look very different from one company to the next.

item.title: Salesforce Einstein
item.description:
Einstein brought AI to Salesforce customers well before generative AI became popular. Predictive features score leads and opportunities, forecast revenue, recommend next best actions, and flag at-risk accounts, using each company’s own CRM data. Einstein Discovery finds patterns and suggests what drives outcomes, and bots and analytics features extend the same ideas to service and marketing.

With generative AI, Einstein has expanded to write emails, summarize records and cases, and generate service replies, grounded in customer data and protected by the Einstein Trust Layer, which masks sensitive information and prevents customer data from being used to train outside models. The conversational assistant evolved into Agentforce, which builds autonomous agents on the same foundation, so Einstein now refers to a mix of older predictive features and the generative AI infrastructure.

item.title: SalesLoft
item.description:
Salesloft helps sales teams organize outbound and follow-up work. Reps follow cadences, which are structured sequences of emails, calls, and social touches, and the platform tells them who to contact next and records each activity in the CRM. Managers can see which messages and sequences generate replies and meetings, and coach reps with call recordings and analytics.

The platform has expanded into revenue orchestration. Conversation intelligence records and summarizes calls, deal management tracks stage progress and risk, and forecasting tools combine pipeline data with engagement signals. Salesloft acquired Drift for conversational marketing and has combined with Clari, a revenue forecasting company, to build a broader revenue platform. AI assistants prepare meeting briefs, draft messages, and suggest next steps.

item.title: SAP Ariba
item.description:
SAP Ariba helps large organizations buy what they need in an organized way. Procurement teams use it to find and evaluate suppliers, run sourcing events, manage contracts, process purchase orders and invoices, and monitor supplier risk. The Ariba Network connects buyers and suppliers electronically, so orders and invoices flow between systems without manual entry.

AI is being added to reduce manual work. SAP’s assistant, Joule, can help users search for information, draft sourcing documents, and answer questions about spend, and features analyze contracts, recommend suppliers, and flag unusual transactions. Integration with SAP’s ERP and other systems provides a connected view of purchasing, and spend analytics reveal savings opportunities.

item.title: Scale AI
item.description:
Scale AI built its business on a simple observation: AI models need huge amounts of well-labeled data, and quality control at scale is hard. It combines software with a large network of human contributors and experts to annotate images, video, text, and sensor data. Early customers included self-driving car developers, and the company grew by supplying training data to the biggest AI labs.

Today much of its work involves large language models. Scale provides human feedback data used in reinforcement learning, expert-written examples for fine-tuning, and evaluations that test models for accuracy and safety. Its tools help companies manage data pipelines, and a generative AI platform lets enterprises customize models on their own data. Public-sector work includes AI systems for defense and government agencies, and the company runs public leaderboards that rank models on hard tests.

item.title: SEMrush
item.description:
Semrush bundles many marketing tools in one subscription. Users research keywords, audit websites, track rankings, analyze backlinks, spy on competitors’ traffic and ads, and plan content, all from a shared dashboard. It is widely used by agencies and in-house teams.

AI features help with writing and analysis. A writing assistant drafts and optimizes content, AI tools summarize data and suggest actions, and newer products track how brands appear in AI-generated answers from chat assistants, a growing concern for search marketers. Reports and integrations suit client work.

item.title: ServiceNow
item.description:
ServiceNow began as an IT service management tool and became a general workflow platform for large organizations. Employees and customers submit requests, such as a laptop problem, a payroll question, or a customer complaint, and the platform routes, tracks, and resolves them using defined workflows. Companies use it as a system of record and action across IT operations, HR, legal, security, and customer service.

AI is central to its current strategy. Now Assist adds generative AI to summarize cases, draft replies, and help agents find answers, and AI agents can take on tasks such as triaging incidents and fulfilling requests with minimal human intervention. The company acquired Moveworks, whose employee assistant is intended to become the front door to the platform, and offers tools to govern and monitor agents across the enterprise.

item.title: Shopify
item.description: Shopify lets someone start an online store without building the software behind it. You choose a theme, add products, set up payments and shipping, and the platform handles hosting, the checkout, and tax and currency settings. The same system also covers in-person sales through point-of-sale hardware, so a shop can manage online and physical inventory together. Everything from a one-person side business to large brands runs on it, and Shop Pay, its accelerated checkout, is used well beyond Shopify’s own stores.

item.title: SimilarWeb
item.description:
Similarweb lets you look at the performance of sites you do not own. Enter a domain, and it shows estimated monthly visits, traffic sources such as search, social, and direct, top keywords, referring sites, audience demographics, and engagement metrics like time on site. Data comes from a mix of panels, partnerships, and public sources, modeled to produce estimates. This helps in benchmarking competitors and finding growth opportunities.

The platform covers more than websites. It tracks app usage and downloads, advertising, and market segments, and ranks sites within categories. Recent additions include tracking how brands and sites are cited and visited through AI chatbots, reflecting the way people increasingly use AI assistants instead of search. Investors use the data to spot trends in company performance before financial reports, and sales teams use it to find leads.

item.title: Sisense
item.description:
Sisense helps organizations analyze data and share insights. Analysts connect data sources, build models and dashboards, and users explore results in a browser. Its strength is embedding: software companies place Sisense charts and analytics inside their products for customers.

AI features include asking questions in plain language, forecasting, and automatic detection of unusual patterns, plus a generative assistant that builds dashboards. The platform works with cloud data warehouses and offers an API-first approach.

item.title: Square
item.description:
Square is known for its card readers and registers. A small business accepts payments in person, online, or by invoice, tracks inventory, and manages staff and payroll from a single account. Hardware ranges from a simple reader to full countertop systems.

Additional services include appointments, loyalty programs, marketing, and small business loans based on sales. AI assistance writes item descriptions, generates insights from sales data, and answers business questions.

Square charges processing fees per transaction and sells hardware, with paid software tiers for advanced features. It has a free plan for basic use. Alternatives include Toast for restaurants, Clover, Shopify POS, Stripe Terminal, and SumUp. Square suits small retail and food businesses.

item.title: Stamped.io
item.description:
Stamped helps online stores build trust. After a purchase, it emails customers asking for reviews, collects star ratings with photos or videos, and displays them on product pages and in search results with structured data. Social proof improves conversion rates, and review requests can be automated and timed, with options to send coupons for leaving a review.

The platform also offers loyalty and referral programs. Customers earn points for purchases and actions, redeem rewards, and refer friends, which encourages repeat business. AI features summarize reviews into key themes, surface what customers love or dislike, and help merchants respond. Reports show review volume, ratings, and the effect on sales, and integrations connect with email, helpdesk, and ads tools.

item.title: Stampli
item.description:
Stampli keeps the conversation about an invoice attached to the invoice. When a bill arrives, teams discuss it in context, approvers sign off, and the payment goes out, with no hunting through email threads. It connects to accounting systems and does not require replacing them.

Billy the Bot reads invoices, suggests coding and approvals based on past behavior, and flags anomalies. Payment tools handle payments and cards, and the platform provides audit trails and reporting.

item.title: Tableau
item.description:
Tableau is known for making data exploration feel visual and quick. Analysts connect to databases, spreadsheets, and cloud data warehouses, then drag fields onto a canvas to build charts, maps, and dashboards without writing code. It handles large data volumes well, and its interactivity lets viewers filter, drill down, and compare in ways static reports cannot. It is widely used in finance, healthcare, retail, government, and education.

Salesforce owns Tableau and has built AI into it. Tableau Pulse sends personalized, plain-language insights about key metrics to the people who care about them, and flags unusual changes without anyone opening a dashboard. Tableau Agent helps users build visualizations and analyze data by chatting with the tool. Tableau Prep cleans and combines data, and the platform integrates with Salesforce data and its Data Cloud.

item.title: Talkdesk
item.description:
Talkdesk provides the software contact centers use to handle calls and messages. Customers reach an agent by phone, chat, or messaging, and the platform routes them, records interactions, and reports on performance. Cloud delivery makes setup quicker than legacy systems.

AI is part of each layer. Virtual agents resolve common requests, agent assist suggests replies and surfaces knowledge during calls, quality tools score conversations automatically, and forecasting helps schedule staff. Industry versions serve healthcare, financial services, and retail.

item.title: ThoughtSpot
item.description:
ThoughtSpot built its product around search. Instead of building reports by dragging fields, business users type a question such as sales by region last quarter, and ThoughtSpot generates the right chart from the connected data warehouse, with the ability to drill down and refine. This lowers the barrier for people who are not analysts and reduces the queue of requests for data teams.

Generative AI has expanded the approach. Spotter acts as an AI analyst that understands questions in conversation, runs analyses, explains results, and proposes follow-up questions, while agents can answer questions inside other tools. Liveboards combine charts into shareable dashboards that update from live data, and an embedded analytics offering lets companies put these capabilities in their own products.

item.title: Tipalti
item.description:
Tipalti automates accounts payable for growing companies. Suppliers and partners onboard through a portal that collects tax forms and payment details, invoices are captured and approved, and Tipalti pays them in the local currency and method across many countries.

Compliance is a main benefit: the platform handles tax documentation, sanctions screening, and reporting, which is hard for companies paying people worldwide. AI reads invoices, flags anomalies, and helps reconcile payments in accounting systems.

item.title: Toast
item.description:
Toast serves the restaurant industry. Servers take orders on handheld devices, kitchen displays route tickets, guests pay at the table or online, and managers track sales, labor, and inventory. Online ordering, delivery integrations, and loyalty programs are part of the ecosystem.

Data and AI support operations. Sales forecasts help schedule staff, menu analytics show what sells, and assistants help write menu descriptions and answer business questions. Payroll and team management tools extend the suite.

item.title: Unbounce AI
item.description:
Unbounce helps marketers create landing pages that convert. A drag-and-drop builder and templates make it possible to publish pages without developers, with popups and sticky bars to capture leads on websites. Marketers connect pages to ad campaigns and test variants to find what performs best.

AI is a core part. Smart Copy generates headlines and body text from a brief, and Smart Traffic uses machine learning to send each visitor to the variant they are most likely to convert on, based on their attributes, which can improve results faster than a standard A/B test. Newer tools analyze pages and suggest improvements, and AI builder features create a page from a prompt.

item.title: WooCommerce
item.description:
WooCommerce is the most widely used way to run a store on WordPress. You install the plugin, add products, set up payments, shipping, and taxes, and manage orders from the WordPress dashboard. Because it is open source, you own the store and the data, host it where you want, and can modify anything with code or extensions.

The ecosystem is its strength. Thousands of themes and extensions add subscriptions, bookings, memberships, marketplaces, and connections to accounting and marketing tools. AI extensions can write product descriptions, suggest recommendations, and help with support, and Automattic’s own tools plus third-party plugins fill the gaps. Many agencies build custom stores on top of it.

item.title: Workday
item.description:
Workday began as cloud HR software and expanded into financials. Large employers use it to keep employee records, run payroll and benefits, manage recruiting and performance, plan headcount and budgets, and close the books. Having HR and finance on one data model helps companies tie workforce decisions to costs.

AI shows up across the suite. It suggests candidates and skills matches, flags attrition risks, helps managers with planning, and drafts job descriptions and summaries. Workday has also introduced AI agents that take on tasks inside its apps, along with an agent management layer so that companies can control what those agents may do. It has bought AI companies to extend this, including some that build agent platforms.

item.title: Yodlee
item.description:
Yodlee lets financial apps pull in customers’ account data. A budgeting tool, lender, or wealth platform can use Yodlee’s APIs to link to thousands of financial institutions, retrieve balances and transactions, and keep them updated. That saves each company from building separate connections to every bank.

Beyond raw data, Yodlee enriches transactions. Machine learning cleans merchant names, assigns categories, and flags patterns, and analytics products use aggregated data to describe consumer spending trends. Account verification and income checks help lenders confirm information, and the company supports open banking rules in regions where they exist.

item.title: Yotpo
item.description:
Yotpo helps online stores build trust and repeat business. It collects reviews with photos, shows them on product pages and in search, and runs loyalty programs and referral offers. SMS and email tools extend marketing.

AI summarizes reviews into themes, flags issues, and drafts responses, and analytics tie content to conversion. Integrations cover Shopify, BigCommerce, and other platforms.

Yotpo has a free tier and paid plans that scale with orders. Alternatives include Okendo, Judge.me, Stamped.io, Klaviyo, and Trustpilot. Yotpo suits growing online stores.

item.title: Zendesk
item.description:
Zendesk is one of the most widely used help desk systems. Customer messages from email, web chat, phone, WhatsApp, and social media become tickets in a shared workspace, where they can be routed, prioritized, and tracked against service targets. A help center and community forum let customers find answers themselves, and reports show response times and satisfaction. It scales from small support teams to large contact centers.

The current product is built around AI. AI agents take on requests from start to finish, answering from help articles and past conversations, and taking actions in connected systems when allowed. A copilot assists human agents by suggesting replies, summarizing long threads, and flagging urgent or unhappy customers. The platform has added contact center, workforce management, and quality assurance tools, and an employee service product that applies the same ideas to internal IT and HR requests.

item.title: Zeni
item.description:
Zeni provides outsourced finance for startups. Companies connect their bank accounts, and Zeni handles bookkeeping, accounts payable, tax, and CFO services, with a dashboard showing cash, burn, and runway in real time. Humans check the AI’s work.

The service replaces a part-time accountant or finance hire for early-stage companies. Monthly reports help founders and investors understand the business.

Zeni is a subscription service. Alternatives include Pilot, Bench, Puzzle, Digits, and a traditional accountant. Zeni suits startups wanting outsourced finance.

item.title: Zillow
item.description:
Zillow is where many people begin looking for a home. Listings for sale and rent appear on maps and lists with photos, price history, taxes, and school details, and users can filter by price, size, and features, save searches, and get alerts when matching homes appear. Agents and landlords pay to advertise or manage listings.

Its signature feature is the Zestimate, an automated estimate of a home’s value based on public records, market data, and a machine learning model. It is useful as a rough guide but can be off for individual homes, and sellers should not treat it as an appraisal. Zillow also offers mortgage and agent referral services, rental tools, and an AI-powered search that accepts natural language descriptions.

item.title: Zoho
item.description:
Zoho builds a wide range of business applications on its own platform. Companies can use Zoho CRM for sales, Books for accounting, Desk for support, Projects for work tracking, Mail for email, People for HR, and dozens of other apps, many of which integrate with one another. Zoho One bundles the whole suite for a single per-user price.

Zia is the AI layer. It predicts which leads are likely to convert, detects anomalies in data, drafts replies, and answers questions in natural language, and Zoho has added a generative assistant and agents that can act across apps. The company also supports the option of running models on its own infrastructure for customers who want data kept in their region.

item.title: Zoho CRM
item.description:
Zoho CRM covers the normal work of sales: tracking leads and contacts, managing deals through a pipeline, logging calls and emails, and forecasting revenue. It supports multiple channels, including phone, email, live chat, and social media, and lets you build custom modules and fields so it can reflect how a business actually sells. Workflow rules, assignment rules, and blueprints enforce a consistent sales process without manual follow-up.

Zia is the AI layer. It scores leads by how likely they are to convert, predicts which deals will close, spots unusual activity, and recommends the best time to contact a prospect. It can answer questions in plain language, summarize records, and help draft emails. Because Zoho builds its own models, it positions this as a cost-effective alternative to enterprise AI add-ons. Integrations connect with Zoho’s other products such as Campaigns, Books, and Desk, and with outside tools through a marketplace.

item.title: ZoomInfo
item.description:
ZoomInfo provides one of the largest databases of business contacts and companies. Sales and marketing teams search by title, industry, company size, location, and technology to build lists, and see verified email addresses, direct phone numbers, org charts, and firmographic details. Intent data shows which companies are researching topics related to a product, helping teams reach out when interest is high.

The platform has expanded from data into a workflow product. It includes tools for sales engagement, marketing advertising, conversation intelligence through Chorus, and enrichment that keeps CRM records up to date automatically. AI features include assistants that research accounts, draft outreach, and recommend who to contact, and agents that handle prospecting tasks. It integrates with Salesforce, HubSpot, and other systems.

item.title: Zowie
item.description:
Zowie focuses on online retail support. Its AI agent connects to a store’s order system, answers questions about delivery and returns, processes simple actions, and hands off tricky cases to staff. It works across chat, email, and messaging channels.

The platform emphasizes decision-making that follows a brand’s policies, and gives support managers tools to review and adjust behavior. Analytics show resolution rates and topics.

Zowie is sold on subscription. Alternatives include Gorgias, Intercom Fin, Ada, Netomi, and Zendesk AI agents. Zowie suits e-commerce support teams.

item.title: Aisera
item.description: Aisera provides AI agents for internal and external service desks. Employees can ask for help with IT issues, such as resetting a password or requesting software, or HR questions, such as time off policies, and the agent resolves the request by taking actions in connected systems instead of simply pointing to articles. For customers, similar agents handle support inquiries. The goal is to reduce the number of tickets that reach human staff.

item.title: Ashby
item.description:
Ashby brings together tools that recruiting teams often buy separately. The core is an applicant tracking system for jobs, candidates, and interview plans. Around it sit scheduling that coordinates interviewers automatically, a CRM for sourcing and nurturing talent, and an analytics layer that shows pipeline health, time to hire, and source effectiveness.

AI features handle repetitive work, such as summarizing candidates, drafting outreach, and taking notes in interviews. Structured scorecards and interview plans promote consistent evaluation, and reporting is built into the product rather than added on, which analytics-minded recruiting teams like.

item.title: Attio
item.description:
Attio starts from the idea that every company sells differently. Instead of fixed objects like leads and opportunities, teams build their own structures, such as customers, partners, or investors, and link them. The interface feels more like a spreadsheet and a database than a traditional CRM, so it is easier to reshape.

Data fills in with little typing. Attio connects to email and calendar to log interactions, enriches company and contact details, and shows the strength of relationships. AI features summarize accounts, answer questions about the pipeline, and fill in fields from conversations. Workflow automation moves records, sends notifications, and updates data.

item.title: Beamery
item.description:
Beamery treats talent like a relationship, not a one-off hire. Recruiters build pools of potential candidates, track interactions, run campaigns to stay in touch, and see who might fit upcoming roles. The same system can surface current employees for internal moves, which helps companies fill jobs from within.

Its AI builds around skills. It infers skills from resumes and profiles, maps them to a company’s roles, and recommends matches for jobs and development. Workforce planning tools help leaders see skill gaps and plan hiring or training. Integrations connect with applicant tracking systems such as Workday and SuccessFactors.

item.title: Bloomreach
item.description:
Bloomreach serves online retailers. Its discovery product powers site search, category pages, and recommendations, using machine learning to understand what shoppers mean, rank products, and personalize results. Merchandisers can set rules and see how changes affect sales.

The platform also includes engagement tools. A customer data platform unifies behavior across channels, and marketing automation sends email, SMS, and push messages triggered by actions. Content management supports headless sites. AI assistants help marketers build campaigns and analyze performance.

item.title: Braze
item.description:
Braze helps brands talk to customers on the channels where they spend time. Marketers segment users by behavior, design journeys in a visual canvas, and send messages triggered by actions such as opening an app, abandoning a cart, or reaching a milestone. Real-time data means messages respond to what is happening now.

AI features improve targeting and creation. Predictive models estimate who might churn or buy, optimization chooses the best send time and channel for each person, and generative tools help write subject lines and copy. Analytics measure the effect of campaigns on retention and revenue.

item.title: Cleanlab
item.description:
Cleanlab starts from the idea that model quality depends on data quality. Real datasets contain mistakes: images with wrong labels, duplicated examples, and outliers. Cleanlab’s open-source library uses statistical methods and model predictions to find the examples most likely to be wrong, so a team can correct them instead of reviewing everything.

The commercial platform, Cleanlab Studio, extends this with a no-code interface for cleaning and improving datasets and training models on the result. The company has also moved into reliability for generative AI, offering tools to score the trustworthiness of language model outputs and catch hallucinations in production systems.

item.title: CleverTap
item.description:
CleverTap serves brands with mobile apps and large user bases. It collects behavioral data such as app opens, purchases, and feature use, builds segments, and lets marketers send push notifications, email, SMS, WhatsApp, and in-app messages. Journeys can be designed visually so that actions trigger the next message.

AI is used for prediction and optimization. Models estimate which users are likely to churn or convert, choose the best time and channel for each message, and recommend products. A proprietary database designed for large volumes of event data keeps analysis fast, and analytics show retention, funnels, and campaign results.

item.title: Close
item.description:
Close takes the position that sales reps should do their work from one screen. Calls, emails, and texts happen inside the CRM and are logged automatically, so there is less manual data entry and a complete history on each lead. Power dialers let reps work through lists quickly.

Sequences automate multi-step outreach that mixes email, calls, and texts, and workflows keep pipelines moving. AI features transcribe and summarize calls, suggest follow-ups, and score leads, which helps managers coach and helps reps decide where to spend time. Reporting shows activity and results by rep.

item.title: Constructor
item.description:
Constructor serves online retailers that want search and discovery to drive revenue. Its engine powers site search, category pages, and recommendations, ranking products using both shopper behavior and business goals such as margin or inventory. Merchandisers can steer results with rules while the system learns from clicks and purchases.

Additional tools include product quizzes that guide shoppers to the right item, personalization that adapts to each visitor, and analytics that show how discovery affects sales. Generative AI features allow conversational shopping assistants that answer questions and suggest products.

item.title: Copper
item.description:
Copper integrates with the tools its users already work in. Because it lives inside Gmail and connects with Google Calendar, Drive, and Docs, contacts and conversations are logged automatically, so reps do not have to copy information into a separate system.

The CRM covers the usual sales functions: contacts, companies, deals, pipelines, tasks, and reporting. Project management features track work after a deal closes, which suits agencies and service firms. AI features help summarize communication and suggest follow-ups, and workflow automation moves deals through stages.

item.title: Coupa
item.description:
Coupa gives companies control over what they spend. Employees request purchases through approved channels, procurement manages suppliers and contracts, and accounts payable processes invoices and payments. Having it in one system improves visibility and helps enforce policy.

The company’s distinctive asset is aggregated data. With permission, Coupa analyzes anonymized spend across its customer base to benchmark prices, identify supplier risk, and recommend savings. AI features help with spend classification, contract review, and answering questions about spending, and supplier networks connect buyers with vendors.

item.title: Evisort
item.description:
Evisort uses AI to understand contracts. It ingests agreements, identifies clauses and key terms such as renewal dates, payment terms, and liability limits, and stores them as structured data. Teams can search across thousands of contracts, instead of hunting through PDFs.

It supports the contract lifecycle: drafting from templates, negotiating, tracking obligations, and getting alerts before renewals. Reports show risk and spend across the portfolio. Generative AI helps review contracts against playbooks and suggests changes.

item.title: Folk
item.description:
Folk is a relationship manager for people who find traditional CRMs heavy. Users import contacts from email, LinkedIn, and spreadsheets, organize them into groups, and track conversations and deals in a clean interface. It suits agencies, recruiters, investors, and founders who manage many relationships.

AI and automation reduce the manual work. Enrichment fills in details like company and role, a browser extension saves profiles from LinkedIn, and sequences send personalized emails at scale. AI helps write messages and summarize history, and reminders prompt follow-ups so nobody falls through the cracks.

item.title: Freshsales
item.description:
Freshsales is a sales CRM that keeps lead and deal information in one view. Teams track contacts, run pipelines, and log calls and emails, with a built-in phone and chat so reps can contact prospects without switching tools. Automation moves leads through stages and assigns tasks.

Freddy AI assists with prioritization. It scores leads by likelihood to convert, predicts which deals will close, and suggests next best actions, while generative features draft emails and summarize conversations. Analytics show pipeline health, and integrations connect with Freshdesk, marketing tools, and common business apps.

item.title: Front
item.description:
Front treats shared inboxes like collaborative workspaces. Support, sales, and account teams manage messages from several channels in one place, assign conversations, leave internal comments, and see who is handling what. The interface resembles email, so adoption is easy.

Automation and AI reduce manual work. Rules route messages, tag them, and set priorities, while AI summarizes long threads, suggests replies, and answers common questions. Analytics show response times and workloads, and integrations with CRMs and helpdesk tools provide context.

item.title: Gem
item.description:
Gem helps recruiting teams build pipelines. Recruiters search for candidates across LinkedIn and other sources, add them to talent pools, and send sequences of personalized outreach. A candidate CRM tracks every interaction, so when a role opens, the team can reach people they have already engaged.

Analytics show how sourcing channels perform, how long hiring takes, and where candidates drop out. AI features help with search, writing outreach, and identifying candidates who may be open to new roles. An applicant tracking system component extends the suite for teams that want everything in one place.

item.title: Insider
item.description:
Insider helps brands treat each visitor differently. It collects behavior data across channels, builds unified profiles, and uses them to personalize websites, app experiences, and messages. A marketer can design a journey that reaches a customer by email, then push, then SMS depending on what they do.

The AI layer predicts what people are likely to buy or whether they may churn, recommends products, and optimizes timing and content. The platform also includes tools for search, recommendations, and conversational commerce. It is used heavily by retailers and consumer brands in many regions.

item.title: Iterable
item.description:
Iterable lets marketers build cross-channel journeys. They segment customers by behavior, design workflows in a visual canvas, and send messages triggered by actions, such as signing up, abandoning a cart, or reaching a milestone. Data from websites, apps, and warehouses feeds the profile used for personalization.

AI assists in several areas: optimizing the time a message is sent for each person, predicting engagement, recommending content, and helping generate copy. Experimentation tools test variants, and analytics tie campaigns to outcomes. Integration with data warehouses supports teams that centralize customer data.

item.title: Jiminny
item.description:
Jiminny captures conversations between sales teams and customers. It records calls and meetings, creates transcripts, and uses AI to summarize them, extract action items, and detect topics, objections, and talk ratios. Managers use this to coach reps with specific examples.

Deal insights help forecast. The platform flags risks such as lack of next steps or missing stakeholders, and keeps the CRM updated with notes and fields without manual entry. Search across calls lets teams find how customers talk about competitors or pricing.

item.title: Kinaxis
item.description:
Kinaxis helps large manufacturers and retailers plan and respond. Its platform brings demand, supply, inventory, and capacity into one model that updates together, rather than in separate steps, so planners can test the effect of a disruption or a decision in minutes.

Planners run what-if scenarios, see the impact on service and cost, and collaborate across functions. Machine learning improves demand sensing and supply risk detection, and newer AI agents help summarize issues and recommend actions. Customers include companies in high tech, life sciences, automotive, and consumer goods.

item.title: Kixie
item.description:
Kixie speeds up phone outreach. A power dialer calls through a list automatically, local presence shows numbers with the prospect’s area code to improve answer rates, and voicemail drop leaves a prerecorded message with one click. Calls and texts sync with CRMs such as HubSpot, Salesforce, and Pipedrive.

Automation sends text messages and follow-ups triggered by call outcomes, and a coaching feature lets managers listen in. AI transcribes calls, summarizes them, and gives feedback on conversations. Analytics track activity, connect rates, and results by rep.

item.title: Klevu
item.description:
Klevu improves how online shoppers find products. Instead of matching keywords exactly, its search engine uses natural language processing to interpret queries, handle synonyms and misspellings, and rank results based on relevance and merchandising goals. It works with platforms such as Shopify, Magento, and BigCommerce.

The product also includes category browsing, recommendations, and analytics on what shoppers search for and fail to find. Merchandisers can adjust results with rules, and AI personalization adapts to a shopper’s behavior. A chat-style assistant answers product questions.

item.title: Litera
item.description:
Litera is known for products lawyers use daily. Its comparison software shows exactly what changed between document versions, a core need in contract negotiation, and drafting tools check formatting, cross-references, and defined terms. Other products handle transaction management and closing checklists.

Newer AI features help review documents, summarize them, and spot inconsistencies or risk. The company has combined many acquired products into a suite for law firms and corporate legal departments, and it integrates with Microsoft Word and document management systems.

item.title: Matterport
item.description:
Matterport captures spaces in 3D. A camera or a phone scans a property, and the software stitches the data into a navigable model, a virtual tour where viewers can walk through rooms, take measurements, and view floor plans. Real estate agents use it to show listings, and others use it to document sites.

Beyond tours, the platform serves professional needs. Contractors document existing conditions, insurers record property states, and facility managers keep a digital record of buildings. AI helps generate floor plans, label rooms, and create other outputs from scans.

item.title: Mavenoid
item.description:
Mavenoid focuses on products people have trouble setting up or fixing. Instead of a long manual or a phone queue, customers use an interactive guide that asks questions, narrows down the problem, and walks through steps with pictures and videos. If the guide cannot solve it, it hands off to support with the details collected.

Manufacturers build these flows from their manuals and support data, and AI helps generate and maintain content, answer free-text questions, and spot recurring issues. Analytics show where customers get stuck, which feeds back to product teams.

item.title: Monarch Money
item.description:
Monarch Money brings accounts into one dashboard. Users link banks, cards, loans, and investments, and the app tracks spending, net worth, and recurring bills. Budgets can follow a flexible or category-based model, and goals help save toward targets.

Couples and families can share views and manage budgets together while keeping some accounts private. AI categorizes transactions, spots subscriptions, and gives summaries and insights, and an assistant answers questions about finances. Reports show trends over time.

item.title: Mutiny
item.description:
Mutiny changes what a website says depending on the visitor. If a visitor comes from a target account, an industry, or a campaign, Mutiny swaps in headlines, proof points, and calls to action that fit, using firmographic data and ad information. Marketers set this up in a visual editor without developers.

AI recommends segments and generates alternative copy, then tests variations and reports on conversions. Integrations connect with CRMs, ad platforms, and customer data tools so personalization can follow account-based marketing programs.

item.title: Octane AI
item.description:
Octane AI lets stores add an interactive quiz to their site. Shoppers answer questions about preferences, and the quiz recommends products and captures their answers and contact details. Because customers volunteer the information, it is called zero-party data, and it supports personalized email and text marketing.

The platform integrates with Shopify and marketing tools such as Klaviyo, so quiz results can feed segments and flows. Brands use it for skincare, supplements, food, and other categories where choosing among many products is hard. Analytics show how quizzes affect conversion.

item.title: Oliv AI
item.description:
Oliv AI assists sellers before, during, and after calls. Before a meeting, it gathers context on the account and contacts and drafts a briefing. During the call, it records and transcribes. Afterward, it writes notes, updates the CRM, and drafts follow-up emails.

For managers, it scores deals against frameworks such as MEDDIC and highlights risks and gaps, which supports coaching and forecasting. The product presents these functions as agents that take over routine sales admin.

item.title: Paradox
item.description:
Paradox focuses on hiring for roles with many applicants, such as retail, hospitality, and logistics. Olivia chats with candidates by text or on a career site, asks qualifying questions, answers common questions about the job and company, and books interviews directly on managers’ calendars.

That removes much of the scheduling and screening back and forth that slows recruiting. Candidates get fast responses, and recruiters spend time on interviews instead of coordination. The platform includes an applicant tracking tool and onboarding support.

item.title: Phenom
item.description:
Phenom helps employers attract and manage talent. Its career sites show candidates jobs and content tailored to their interests, a recruiting CRM nurtures talent pools, and tools handle scheduling, chat, and applications. The same platform supports employees through internal job matching and career paths.

AI infers skills from resumes and profiles to match people with roles, recommend jobs, and surface candidates already in the system. Analytics show the hiring funnel and diversity data. The company sells to large enterprises.

item.title: Quantified AI
item.description:
Quantified AI helps sales reps practice before they talk to real customers. A rep enters a simulated conversation with an AI buyer that responds in real time, raises objections, and changes direction, and the system scores the performance on things like discovery, handling pushback, and messaging.

Managers use the results to see who needs coaching and track progress over time, and companies can create scenarios that mirror their own sales motions and products. Practice is available any time, which helps new hires ramp faster than relying only on role-play with colleagues.

item.title: Quantilope
item.description:
Quantilope aims to let research teams run advanced studies without waiting weeks on an agency. Researchers pick from automated methods, such as concept tests, segmentation, pricing studies, and brand tracking, set up the survey, and field it to respondents from a panel. Analysis and charts are generated as data comes in.

The platform’s AI helps design studies, suggests suitable methods, writes summaries of findings, and answers questions about the data. Because methodologies are built in, non-specialists can run studies that would normally need a statistician.

item.title: Remesh
item.description:
Remesh scales the focus group. A moderator poses questions to hundreds of participants at once, and people respond in their own words and then rate each other’s answers, so the group quickly reveals where opinions agree and differ. Responses are analyzed as they arrive.

AI clusters comments into themes, summarizes sentiment, and highlights segments by demographic. Researchers use it for message testing, employee listening, public policy input, and product research. A single session can produce depth and breadth that would take many interviews.

item.title: Revenue.io
item.description:
Revenue.io, formerly RingDNA, combines calling with conversation intelligence. During a call, it listens and surfaces prompts, such as a competitor battlecard or the right answer to a pricing objection. After the call, it transcribes, summarizes, and scores conversations against a playbook.

Managers get coaching insights and forecasting signals. The platform includes a dialer and integrates with Salesforce, so call data flows into the CRM. AI assistants draft follow-ups and update records.

item.title: Salesflare
item.description:
Salesflare fills itself in. It connects to email, calendar, and phone, then builds contact and company profiles with conversation history, social data, and notes, so sales reps do not need to type everything. A timeline shows every interaction with a contact.

Features include pipelines, workflows, email tracking, and sequences, plus an intelligent assistant that nudges reps when a lead has gone quiet. It works with Gmail, Outlook, and a mobile app.

item.title: Sapling
item.description:
Sapling helps support and sales teams write faster and more consistently. As an agent types in the help desk or CRM, Sapling suggests completions based on past replies, fixes grammar and tone, and inserts approved snippets. This reduces typing time and variation.

Managers use quality analytics to monitor response times and consistency, and see how suggestions are used. It integrates with Zendesk, Salesforce, Intercom, and other tools, and offers an API and an AI content detector.

item.title: SeekOut
item.description:
SeekOut builds a searchable database of professionals from public profiles and sources. Recruiters filter by skills, experience, and background, find candidates for roles like engineers and scientists, and reach out with outreach sequences.

AI helps match candidates to jobs and understand skill sets, and analytics show talent pools in a region or company. Diversity filters support recruiting programs, subject to legal rules on how they are used. Products extend to internal talent management for employers.

item.title: Streak
item.description:
Streak adds pipeline management to Gmail. Users create boxes for deals, candidates, or projects, move them through stages, and see all related emails, notes, and files in one place. Because it sits in the inbox, there is little context switching.

Features include mail merge, email tracking, scheduling, shared inboxes, and automations. AI helps summarize threads and draft emails. It suits small teams that already run on Google Workspace.

Streak has a free plan and paid tiers. It is tied to Gmail. Alternatives include Copper, HubSpot, Pipedrive, Close, and Attio. Streak suits small teams working from the inbox.

item.title: Trullion
item.description:
Trullion tackles accounting standards that require reading contracts. For leases and revenue contracts, finance teams must pull terms such as payments, dates, and options into calculations. Trullion’s AI reads documents, extracts the data, and generates the schedules and journal entries.

Each figure links back to its source in the document, which helps auditors verify. The platform integrates with accounting systems and handles changes such as lease modifications. It is used by finance teams and audit firms.

item.title: Vic.ai
item.description:
Vic.ai reads invoices and processes them with little manual input. It extracts data, suggests coding to the correct accounts, routes approvals, and flags unusual items, learning from how accountants correct it. The aim is touchless processing for routine invoices.

It integrates with ERP systems such as NetSuite, SAP, and Microsoft Dynamics, and offers payment and analytics features. Accounting firms and mid-sized to large finance teams use it to cut manual work.

item.title: Averi AI
item.description:
Averi is aimed at early-stage companies with big content goals and small teams. It plans topics, drafts articles, and produces supporting copy such as landing pages and social posts, using information about the company’s product and audience to keep content on message.

The idea is to give a founder something like a content department: a planner who chooses what to write, a writer who drafts, and an editor workflow for review. Output is positioned around ranking in search and being cited in AI answers, which are goals that depend on quality and on the site’s authority.

item.title: Clay
item.description:
Clay works like a spreadsheet for sales and marketing data. You start with a list of companies or people, and Clay adds columns that look up information, such as emails, job titles, funding, technologies used, and recent news, pulling from many data providers. Its waterfall enrichment tries one source after another until it finds a result, which improves coverage over relying on a single vendor.

The AI part is a web research agent that can visit sites and answer questions you define for each row, for example whether a company has a mobile app or what it sells. Results feed into AI-written emails and messages tailored to each prospect, and workflows push the finished leads into CRMs and outreach tools like HubSpot, Salesforce, Smartlead, or Outreach. Growth teams use it to build very specific lists and trigger outreach when signals appear.

item.title: Competitor Analyzer
item.description:
Competitor Analyzer helps small teams keep an eye on the market without a full-time analyst. You enter your competitors, and the tool watches their websites, social accounts, content, and in some cases pricing, then summarizes what changed in a weekly digest. The aim is to save the time spent checking sites by hand.

Typical uses include spotting a rival’s new feature or campaign, tracking pricing changes, and gathering material for positioning. AI summaries make the digests quick to read and highlight notable changes. The tool is positioned as simpler and cheaper than enterprise competitive intelligence platforms.

item.title: Cora Intelligence
item.description:
Cora is meant to stand in for a junior sales development rep. A founder describes the ideal customer, and the tool searches for matching prospects, researches them, and writes personalized messages. The goal is to generate conversations without a dedicated hire.

This kind of tool appeals to small companies that need pipeline but lack the budget or time for a sales team. Results depend on how clearly the target customer is defined and how good the messaging is. Automated outreach also has to comply with email rules and can harm a sender’s reputation if poorly targeted.

item.title: Crayon
item.description:
Crayon helps companies keep an eye on their rivals. It continuously monitors thousands of data points, such as changes to competitors’ web pages, pricing, messaging, reviews, hiring patterns, and press coverage, and alerts the team when something meaningful changes. Instead of manually checking competitor sites, product marketers receive a feed of updates they can review and share.

The platform turns the data into usable materials. Teams build battlecards that give sales reps talking points against each competitor, and distribute them in the CRM or in chat tools such as Slack. Analytics track which competitive content is used in deals, and AI summarizes changes, drafts updates, and filters noise. Win-loss insights connect competitive information to outcomes.

item.title: Cresh
item.description:
Cresh is built for early-stage business research. A user describes an idea or market, and several AI agents search sources, gather information, and assemble a report covering competitors, market size, customer needs, and risks. The aim is a fast first pass that would otherwise require manual searching.

Founders use it to test ideas before investing time, and analysts use it to build starting briefs. Reports from AI research tools can contain errors and unsupported claims, so figures and sources should be checked before decisions or investor materials rely on them.

item.title: Denovo
item.description:
Denovo aims to shorten the path from idea to launched business. A user describes what they want to start, and the platform helps produce a business plan, suggests names and branding, generates a website, and walks through setup tasks such as registering the company. Putting these steps in one tool reduces the number of services a beginner must find and learn.

The target is people who have never started a company, or who want to test a side project quickly. AI-generated plans and sites provide a starting point, and users still need to validate demand with real customers and check legal requirements in their location.

item.title: Drift
item.description: Drift popularized the idea of replacing a website contact form with a live conversation. A chat widget greets visitors, asks a few questions, and either answers them, routes them to the right salesperson, or books a meeting on the spot. For B2B companies with long sales cycles, the goal was to catch interested visitors while they were still on the site instead of waiting for them to fill out a form and wait for a reply.

item.title: Eightfold AI
item.description:
Eightfold AI treats talent as a graph of skills. Its models read resumes, job descriptions, and employee profiles, infer skills, and match people to roles based on what they can do and are likely to learn, not just on keywords or job titles. Recruiters use it to find candidates in a company’s applicant database and external sources, and employees can see roles and learning paths that fit their skills.

The platform extends across the employee lifecycle. Modules cover talent acquisition, talent management, internal mobility, and workforce planning, with analytics that show skill gaps and diversity trends. Agent-style features automate steps such as screening and scheduling. It integrates with applicant tracking and HR systems such as Workday and SAP SuccessFactors.

item.title: Evalyze
item.description:
Evalyze aims to make fundraising more systematic. A founder uploads a pitch deck, and the tool reviews it for clarity, story, and typical investor concerns, then suggests improvements. It also helps identify investors whose focus matches the company’s stage and sector.

For first-time founders, structured feedback is useful because many lack access to experienced advisors. Matching tools can narrow a long list of investors to those most likely to be interested, which saves time on outreach.

item.title: GoAI
item.description:
GoAI aims to give individual investors some of the research help professionals have. A user searches a company or asks a question, and the tool pulls financial data, summarizes earnings calls and filings, and highlights notable insider trades. Answers are written in plain language to be readable for non-experts.

Such tools save time reading long documents, but they do not predict the market. AI summaries can contain errors, so important figures should be checked against filings. Past results do not guarantee future performance, and nothing a tool generates should be treated as a recommendation.

item.title: HireVue
item.description:
HireVue lets candidates complete interviews on their own schedule. Employers set up structured questions, candidates record video answers, and recruiters review them later, which saves scheduling time when hiring many people. The platform has expanded to include game-based and skills assessments, live interviews, text-based chat for scheduling and screening, and tools for coding interviews.

Its use of AI has been controversial. HireVue once analyzed facial expressions and voice in interviews, which drew criticism from privacy and civil rights groups, and it dropped facial analysis. Today it describes using structured scoring based on what candidates say and on job-relevant skills, and publishes audits and explanations of its models. Regulations in places such as New York City and Illinois now require notice, consent, or bias audits for automated hiring tools.

item.title: Instantly
item.description:
Instantly is built for outbound email at scale. You connect as many sending accounts as you like, and the platform rotates them to spread volume, which helps keep each account within safe sending limits. An automated warm-up network exchanges emails between accounts to build sender reputation, and tools check deliverability so campaigns are more likely to reach the inbox. Sequences handle follow-ups and stop when someone replies.

AI and data features add to the core sender. A lead database lets users find prospects by role, industry, and location, AI helps write and personalize email copy, and a unified inbox collects replies from all accounts in one place. Analytics show opens, replies, and bounces, and integrations connect with CRMs and automation tools. Agencies, sales teams, and lead generation businesses are the main users.

item.title: Intuo
item.description:
Intuo helps salespeople prepare. It tracks news and events about accounts, markets, and competitors, filters what matters to the user’s deals, and delivers a short brief with suggested conversation starters. The goal is to replace time spent searching the web before each call.

Account executives and sales leaders use it to stay informed about prospects and to find reasons to reach out. The briefs adapt to the seller’s focus areas, and some features suggest actions or talking points tied to the signals.

item.title: Jason AI
item.description:
Jason AI acts as an automated sales development rep within Reply.io. It finds prospects, writes personalized emails and LinkedIn messages, sends them, and replies to responses to move conversations toward a meeting. It works within Reply.io’s sequencing system, which also handles calls and tasks.

Users give it information about their product and target customers, and Jason builds campaigns. A human can review messages and take over when a lead is interested. The goal is to let small teams reach more prospects without hiring more reps.

item.title: Julius AI
item.description: Julius lets people explore data by asking questions. After uploading a CSV or Excel file, or connecting to a database or Google Sheets, you can ask for things like the average sales by region, a trend over time, or a correlation between two columns. Julius writes and runs code behind the scenes, then shows the result as a chart, a table, or a written explanation, and you can view the code to check what it did.

item.title: Jupid
item.description:
Jupid is accounting help for sole proprietors. Users link their bank accounts and cards, and the app sorts each transaction into the categories used on Schedule C, which is the tax form for self-employment income. It flags business expenses, helps separate personal spending, and keeps a running view of profit.

The tool estimates quarterly taxes and highlights deductions that people often miss, which reduces the scramble at tax time. Reports can be exported to share with an accountant or to use when filing. AI handles the sorting and learns from corrections.

item.title: Lavender
item.description:
Lavender sits in your email composer and gives feedback in real time. As you write a cold email, it gives a score and highlights problems: sentences that are too long, language that sounds salesy, a missing clear ask, or a message that is too focused on you instead of the recipient. It suggests edits and shows how changes affect the score, acting like a coach looking over your shoulder.

Personalization is a second pillar. Lavender can pull in information about the recipient, such as their role, company news, and social posts, and suggest personalized opening lines and talking points. A Chrome extension works in Gmail and Outlook and integrates with sales engagement tools, so it fits existing workflows. Managers can see team-wide analytics and coach reps on writing.

item.title: Lightfield
item.description:
Lightfield rethinks the CRM as a system that fills itself. It connects to email, calendar, and call recordings, and extracts contacts, companies, deals, and notes automatically, so records stay current without reps typing. The aim is to remove the data entry that makes CRMs unpopular.

Beyond capturing data, it uses the context to help with work, such as drafting follow-ups, answering questions about accounts, and surfacing deals that need attention. The team behind it previously built Tome, a presentation tool, before turning to this product.

item.title: MarketAlerts.ai
item.description:
MarketAlerts.ai watches the market on behalf of its users. Investors list their holdings, and the service monitors news, filings, price moves, and other events, sending alerts when something relevant happens and summarizing why it might matter. Some alerts include AI-generated signals about possible actions.

Such tools save time for people who cannot follow the market all day, but they carry risks. AI-generated trade signals are not reliable predictions, markets are unpredictable, and acting on automated signals can lose money. Nothing here is financial advice.

item.title: Obviously AI
item.description:
Obviously AI was built to make machine learning accessible to business users. You upload a CSV or connect a data source, choose the thing you want to predict, such as customer churn, sales, or lead conversion, and the platform tests multiple algorithms, picks the best one, and shows the results in plain language. It highlights which columns most influence the prediction and lets you try what-if scenarios.

Predictions can be exported or sent to other tools, and the platform offers dashboards for sharing insights with teammates. It positions itself for marketing, sales, finance, and operations analysts who have data but no data scientists, and for consultants who need quick models for clients.

item.title: Page Pulse
item.description:
Page Pulse aims to make analytics approachable. A site owner adds a snippet and sees visitors, popular pages, sources, and conversions in a clear dashboard, without needing to learn a complex reporting interface. The focus is on answers to basic questions about what is working.

Typical users are small businesses, bloggers, and agencies that report to clients and want simple summaries. Some AI features explain trends in plain language and suggest improvements.

item.title: Ramp
item.description:
Ramp issues corporate cards and wraps them in software for controlling spending. Companies give employees physical and virtual cards with limits and rules, and receipts are captured and matched automatically through the app. Finance teams see spending in real time and avoid chasing employees for expense reports. Ramp is known for fast growth among startups and mid-sized businesses.

The product has widened into a finance operating system. Bill pay handles vendor invoices, procurement tools manage purchase requests and approvals, and accounting automation categorizes transactions and syncs with systems such as NetSuite, QuickBooks, and Xero. AI agents review expenses against policy, suggest ways to cut costs from vendor spending data, and handle routine tasks such as coding transactions and preparing month-end close.

item.title: Robin AI
item.description:
Robin AI developed tools for lawyers who spend their days reading contracts. Its platform used language models trained on legal text to review agreements, flag risks, suggest edits to bring them in line with a company’s playbook, and answer questions about clauses. It worked in Microsoft Word and was used by in-house legal teams and law firms for routine commercial agreements such as NDAs, supplier contracts, and sales terms.

The company also combined software with a managed legal services offering, in which lawyers reviewed work and handled volume for clients. That mix aimed to deliver quick, reliable turnaround, with AI doing the first pass and humans checking. It gained attention for fast growth and for partnerships and funding in the legal AI boom.

item.title: Spellbook
item.description:
Spellbook was built to meet lawyers where they work: in Word. As you draft or review a contract, it suggests language, flags missing or risky terms, and proposes edits as tracked changes. You can ask it questions about a clause, have it compare a draft with your standard positions, or generate a first draft from a prompt, always inside the document you are working on.

Features extend to the review and negotiation steps. A library of benchmarks shows how a term compares to market standards, a playbook feature lets firms encode their preferred positions for checking contracts, and agent-style workflows can run multi-step tasks such as reviewing a set of agreements. It’s used by law firms and in-house teams, particularly for transactional work, and builds on leading language models with legal-specific prompts and data.

item.title: The Influencer AI
item.description:
The Influencer AI generates a virtual person who can appear in ads, product demos, and social posts. A brand creates or selects a character and the tool produces images and videos of that character holding products, talking to the camera, or appearing in scenes, with consistent looks across content.

The pitch is cost and speed. Producing varied creative with real models requires scheduling, travel, and fees, while AI can generate many variations quickly for testing ads. Features include scripts, voices, and lip-synced video.

item.title: THEO
item.description:
THEO helps with the thinking behind a brand. A user provides information about their company and competitors, and the AI analyzes the market, identifies open positioning territories, and proposes strategic actions with reasoning. The output can feed workshops and strategy documents.

It targets strategists, agencies, and marketing leaders who want a faster starting point than a blank canvas. AI suggestions depend on the inputs and cannot replace customer research or judgment.

item.title: Tidio
item.description:
Tidio targets small online businesses that want to answer customers quickly without a big support team. A chat widget on the website lets visitors ask questions, and the tool collects messages from chat, email, and social channels in one inbox. Visual chatbot flows handle common tasks, such as collecting contact details, recommending products, and recovering abandoned carts.

Lyro, its AI agent, answers customer questions using the store’s help content and product data, and hands off to a human when needed. Automations trigger messages based on visitor behavior, and integrations with Shopify, WordPress, WooCommerce, and others bring in order and product information. Tidio is aimed at ease of setup, and most stores can install it in minutes.

item.title: Watermelon
item.description:
Watermelon is aimed at support teams that want automation without engineering. They design conversation flows in a visual builder, train the bot on help content, and connect it to chat channels such as websites and WhatsApp. Complex cases transfer to humans with the conversation history.

AI features answer free-form questions from a knowledge base, and analytics show resolution rates and topics. The platform includes a shared inbox for agents, so the bot and humans work in one system.
